### Overview This dataset shows projections of aragonite saturation in the world’s oceans from 2006-2099. The aragonite saturation state (Ωarag) is commonly used to track ocean acidification because it is a measure of carbonate ion concentration, which indicates the availability of the calcium carbonate that is widely used by marine calcifiers, from lobsters to clams to starfish. Aragonite itself is the building block of stony corals that are the primary framework and habitat builders of coral reef ecosystems. Corals and other calcifiers are most likely to survive and reproduce when the aragonite saturation state is greater than 4. Saturation above 3.5 is adequate; above 3 is considered marginal, with growth difficult. When the saturation state falls below 3, these organisms are in danger. Below 1, reefs, shells, and other aragonite structures begin to dissolve entirely. These projections are based on future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 8.5. The RCP 8.5 scenario presumes no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. More information on these scenarios can be found [here](http://tntcat.iiasa.ac.at:8787/RcpDb/dsd?Action=htmlpage&page=about). The projections have a spatial resolution of 1 degree, and cover the entire globe, although the significance of carbonate ion concentrations outside of areas containing warm-water coral reefs is beyond the scope of this discussion. The dataset was created by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data and Information Service (NESDIS) as part of their Coral Reef Watch program. It was created as a way to both incite and inform discussions about the effects of climate change on coral reefs. These may be dramatic: the predicted acidification during the 21st century would be a greater change than possibly at any time in the last 300 million years. Coral reefs are among the most biologically rich and productive ecosystems on earth and provide valuable ecosystem benefits to millions of people in coastal areas. They are, however, widely threatened by both local threats (such as overfishing, pollution, and direct physical damage) and the global threats of ocean warming and acidification. These have already caused widespread damage to most of the world’s coral reefs, resulting in reduced areas of living coral, increased algal cover, diminished species diversity, and lower fish abundance, as well as degraded economic and social benefits to many coastal communities. ### Methodology Ensembles of climate models were used to generate projections of the year when severe coral bleaching events will start to occur annually, and of changes in Ωarag. The models were used to generate projected monthly data for the following variables: sea surface temperature (SST), surface pressure of CO₂, pH, and salinity. Each model independently generated monthly data for the listed variables, and these model outputs were then adjusted to the mean and annual cycle of observations of SST based on the [OISST V2 1982‐2005 climatology](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/oisst/optimum-interpolation-sea-surface-temperature-oisst-v20). Projections were generated for all four RCP scenarios (known as RCP 2.6, 4.5, 6.0, and 8.5); those corresponding to RCP 8.5 were produced using 9 fully coupled models in the [Coupled Model Intercomparison Project 5 (CMIP5)](https://esgf-node.llnl.gov/projects/cmip5/). For each model, Ωarag was computed independently on the basis of those four key variables, as forecast by that same model, by adopting the routines of the Matlab program [CO2SYS](https://cdiac.ess-dive.lbl.gov/ftp/oceans/co2sys/CO2SYS_calc_MATLAB_v1.1/). Finally, the calculated Ωarag projections from all models were combined, as averaging over multiple models can reduce errors and generally increases the accuracy, skill, and consistency of model forecasts. All modeled data were remapped to a 1º resolution. Some model outputs were reduced to a sub-set of only reef locations. These were obtained from the United Nations Environmental Program-World Conservation Monitoring Center’s [Millennium Coral Reef Mapping Project Seascape](http://imars.usf.edu/MC/). A cell was counted as a reef cell if it contained any tropical coral reefs according to the original Seascape database. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/gcb.12394). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Ωarag is projected annually, but shown on Resource Watch only at decadal intervals. The full dataset also includes projections of coral bleaching and reductions in calcification, as well as additional ocean acidification projections, under four climate scenarios (RCP 2.6, 4.5, 6.0, 8.5). For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/ocn_006_projected_ocean_acidification). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

We recommend using [this dataset](6b523d76-ca2d-4059-b0a6-d90a6b8ba5a6) as a replacement.**_ The GLW is a global livestock mapping project by the Food and Agriculture Organization's Animal Production and Health Division (FAO-AGA). The data shows livestock distributions for the year 2006 at a 0.05° resolution.The methodology and sources of data are fully described in a document entitled: "The Gridded Livestock of the World. FAO (2007)". In summary, for each country the most recent available sub-national livestock census data and corresponding administrative boundaries have been collected. These are then converted into densities, excluding land unsuitable for livestock (either monogastric or ruminant), to provide the 'observed' data. The data are then disaggregated based on statistical relations with some environmental variables in similar agro-ecological zones to produce the 'predicted' distribution. The predicted data are further manipulated to match national census totals for the year 2000 according to the FAOSTAT database. The project also includes: a global network of data providers on livestock and sub-national boundaries; an Oracle database in which these data are managed and processed; a system for predicting livestock distributions based on environmental data and an interactive web application, the Global Livestock Production and Health Atlas (GLiPHA), through which data are viewed and disseminated. The files are in a raster GRID format. Pixel values represent actual densities (per square kilometre). These data have been produced by FAO's Animal Production and Health Division in collaboration with ERGO and the TALA research group, University of Oxford, UK. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. General Description Drought Soil Moisture Anomalies (SMA) at 12.5km from soil moisture data of EUMETSAT - TU Wien ASCAT-SSM-CDR-12.5km version 7 (H120) climate data record dataset over Europe, monthly time-series (2007-2022) The Soil Moisture Anomalies (SMA) dataset provides Z score soil moisture anomalies of the soil moisture dataset of the EUMETSAT - TU Wien ASCAT-SSM-CDR-12.5km version 7 (H120). The dataset time spans from March 2007 to December 2022 (to be updated to Version 8, H121, that extends to Aug 2024) for the entire globe (here SMAs provided only for Europe so far). The dataset has direct applicability in analysing the soil moisture alterations from the regional to the global scale, as well as in evaluating the multiple other processes dependent on the evolution of soil moisture not only in the hydrosphere but also in the atmosphere and biosphere. The dataset includes: Monthly time-series: Monthly average of SMA generated with soil moisture data aggregated at 10-day periods ('dekad', corresponding to the 1st, 11th and 21th day of each month) following the approach defined in the European and Global Drought Observatories. Data Details Time period: March 2007 – December 2022 Type of data: Soil Moisture Anomaly (z-scored) of soil moisture data aggregated in 10-day periods How the data was collected or derived: ASCAT-SSM-CDR-12.5km version 7 (H120) with all processing computed using Python packages. Statistical methods used: z-scored soil moisture anomalies. Coordinate reference system: EPSG:4326 Bounding box (Xmin, Ymin, Xmax, Ymax): (-25, 25, 65, 72.5) Spatial resolution: 0.008333 d.d. (1km) Image size: 21600 x 8962 File format: Cloud Optimized Geotiff (COG) format. Support If you discover a bug, artefact, or inconsistency, or if you have a question please contact: jaimegaonagarcia@cnr.it Reference Gaona, J., Bavera, D., Fioravanti, G., Hahn, S., Stradiotti, P., Filippucci, P., ... & Brocca, L. (2024). Soil moisture products consistency for operational drought monitoring in Europe. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences Discussions, 2024, 1-36. description: Marine Ecoregions of the World (MEOW), produced by The Nature Conservancy (TNC) and the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) and modified in 2007, represents broad-scale patterns of species and communities in the ocean. It was designed as a tool for planning conservation across a range of scales and assesses conservation efforts and gaps worldwide. This new biogeographic classification for the world’s coastal and shelf areas draws heavily on the existing global and regional literature. The authors reviewed 230 works in journals, NGO reports, government publications, and other sources to classify these regions. The current system focuses on coast and shelf areas and does not consider realms in pelagic or deep benthic environments. The ecoregional classification relates primarily to coast and shelf biotas for which a 200 m depth contour is an indicative boundary. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. ### Overview This dataset shows projected sea surface height around the world for every year through 2100, relative to average sea surface height during 1986–2005. Sea surface height (SSH) varies geographically: shifting surface winds, the expansion of warming ocean water, and the addition of melting ice can alter ocean currents which, in turn, lead to changes in sea level that vary from place to place. Past and present variations in the distribution of land ice affect the shape and gravitational field of the Earth, which also cause regional fluctuations in sea level. Additional variations in sea level are caused by the influence of more localized processes such as sediment compaction and tectonics. To properly reflect this variability, the projections comprise a time series of 1° resolution geospatial grids. Over relatively short time spans (hours to years), the influence of tides, storms, and climatic variability—such as El Niño—dominates sea level variations. Earthquakes and landslides can also have an effect by causing changes in land height and, sometimes, tsunamis. Over longer time spans (decades to centuries), the influence of climate change—with consequent changes in volume of ocean water and land ice—is the main contributor to sea level change in most regions. Ocean thermal expansion and glacier melting were the dominant contributors to 20th century global mean sea level rise. It is very likely that the rate of sea level rise during the 21st century will exceed the rate observed during 1971–2010. These data were used in the construction of figures for the Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the United Nations body for assessing the science related to climate change. As the IPCC states, "Continued emission of greenhouse gases will cause further warming and long-lasting changes in all components of the climate system, increasing the likelihood of severe, pervasive and irreversible impacts for people and ecosystems." Over recent decades, more than 90% of the net energy increase of the climate system has been stored in the ocean, and its warming provides both strong evidence for and measurement of a changing climate. ### Methodology The final projections for global mean sea level rise represent the sum of anticipated contributions from a number of different sources. These include: ocean heat uptake and the subsequent thermal expansion of seawater; land water storage and changes in land surface characteristics that influence runoff or evapotranspiration rates, such as dams, irrigation schemes, or groundwater depletion; diminishing glaciers; and changes in the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets, including direct outflows of water from melting and icebergs as well as more complex interactions between the sheets, the land surface on which they rest, and the ocean. Annual time series for change in global mean surface air temperature and global mean sea level rise due to thermal expansion in the past and during the 21st century under different emissions scenarios were obtained from a set of 21 Atmosphere–Ocean General Circulation Models (AOGCMs) of the [Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5)](https://pcmdi.llnl.gov/mips/cmip5/). AOGCMs have components representing the ocean, atmosphere, land, and cryosphere, and simulate sea surface height changes resulting from volcanic eruptions and changes in solar irradiance, and from anthropogenic increases in GHGs and aerosols. AOGCMs also exhibit internally generated climate variability, including such patterns as the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and others that affect sea level. As in the real world, ocean density, circulation and sea level are dynamically connected in AOGCMs and evolve together. The overall contribution of an ice mass to sea level involves changes to either its surface mass balance (SMB) or changes in the dynamics of ice flow that affect outflow (i.e., solid ice discharge) to the ocean. SMB is primarily the difference between snow accumulation and the melt and sublimation of snow and ice (ablation). Regional Climate Models (RCMs), which incorporate or are coupled to sophisticated representations of the mass and energy budgets associated with snow and ice surfaces, are now the primary source of ice-sheet SMB projections. The change in Greenland ice sheet SBM was obtained by fitting results from an RCM using input from several CMIP5 AOGCMs For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.climatechange2013.org/images/report/WG1AR5_Ch13SM_FINAL.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Available data include 10 geophysical sources that drive long-term changes in relative SSH: * 5 ice components (Greenland dynamic ice and surface mass balance, Antarctic dynamic ice and surface mass balance, and glaciers), * 3 ocean-related components, all of which are derived from CMIP5 models (dynamic SSH, global thermosteric SSH anomaly, and the inverse barometer effect from the atmosphere), * land water storage (also called terrestrial water), and * glacial isostatic adjustment (as a change in sea level relative to land). In addition to the relatively few fields actually used in the IPCC-AR5 figures, all individual components are available, both as maps of 20-year mean differences (always the 2081-2100 mean minus the 1986-2005 mean), and as time series with the 1986-2005 mean set as the common zero SSH anomaly value. Resource Watch displays the time series of total ensemble mean SSH for emissions scenario RCP 8.5; that same time series, along with those for lower, median, and upper projections, exist for RCP 2.6, 4.5, and 6.0 as well, along the projections from all 21 CMIP5 models. description: ### Overview The dataset represents the count (pieces per square kilometer) and weight (grams per square kilometer) densities of plastic particles floating in the ocean. The data was created from an oceanographic model of floating debris dispersal and calibrated using data from surveys done during 24 expeditions conducted from 2007-2013. The results have been adjusted for a variety of factors like particle fragmentation and wind driven mixing of water. The data is presented in four particle size categories ranging from 0.33 millimeters to >200 millimeters. The final results are shown in raster format at a spatial resolution of 20 kilometers. Plastic pollution is globally distributed across all oceans and is regarded as a major health issue for marine and human life. As plastic degrades it forms microplastics that are often consumed by marine fauna, slowly working up the food chain. In addition, floating plastics can move across oceans and transport species to non-native regions. This study was conducted to help countries understand their impacts on the ocean and to be used in implementing plastic waste reduction policies. It was authored by researchers from a variety of organizations and funded by an array of environmental and educational groups. The data has global coverage and is available at a spatial resolution of 0.2° or about 20 kilometers. ### Methodology To gather the mass and count of the ocean’s plastics, the researchers conducted 24 expeditions (2007–2013) across all five subtropical gyres, coastal Australia, Bay of Bengal, and the Mediterranean Sea. During these expeditions 680 surface net tows and 891 visual survey transects of large plastic debris were conducted. Surface net tows were done using a mesh size of 0.33 millimeters towed at 0.5 to 2 meters below the ocean surface for 15 to 60 minutes. Visual surveys were carried out using dedicated observers viewing 20 meter sections next to the boat noting large floating debris. Debris observations were broken into nine categories, four categories for fishing-related debris: buoy, line, net, and other fishing gear, and five categories for other plastics: bucket, bottle, foamed polystyrene, bag/film, or miscellaneous plastics. All 1,571 mesh and visual surveys included data on plastic counts and 1,333 of them also included data on debris weight. The data was used to create debris estimates and calibrate an oceanographic model based on water movement to show the dispersal of floating debris. The model used to describe oceanic currents was the US Navy’s Hybrid Coordinate Ocean Model (HYCOM). This was combined with a Lagrangian particle-tracking model Pol3DD to mimic how plastic particles move through the ocean. The model assumes that amounts of plastic entering the ocean depends on three principal variables: watershed outfalls, population density, and maritime activity. The results were adjusted to compensate for wind driven mixing of the surface layer that forces plastic particles below the surface. Additionally, conservative estimates for particle fragmentation rates were used when determining particle count. Through this methodology, estimated values were generated for the count and weight of ocean plastic in four size classes: 0.33-1.0 millimeters, 1.01-4.75 millimeters, 4.76-200 millimeters, and >200 millimeters. For full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0111913). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. MHTs reflect groupings of ecoregions with similar biological, chemical, and physical characteristics. The MHTs refer to the dynamics of ecological systems and the broad habitat structures that define them. These groupings can provide a structured framework for examining and comparing the diversity of life in terrestrial systems. MHTs are broadly broken down by latitude, ranging from boreal and tundra, temperature, and tropical regions. Temperate and tropical forests are further broken down into broadleaf and conifers. These regions are also distinguished by moisture level, ranging from desert, xeric, and dry, to moist habitats. Finally, shrublands are distinguished by elevation, from high altitude montane shrublands to flooded lowlands. The ecoregions, originally developed by Olson and Dinerstein (2002), Bailey (1995), and Environment Canada (Wiken 1986), were modified by TNC. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. The Freshwater Ecoregions of the World (FEOW), an updated version of the original data set produced by The Nature Conservancy (TNC) and the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), provides a global biogeographic regionalization of the Earth's freshwater biodiversity. The freshwater major habitat types (MHTs) reflect groupings of ecoregions with similar biological, chemical, and physical characteristics and are roughly equivalent to biomes for terrestrial systems. The MHTs refer to the dynamics of ecological systems and the broad habitat structures that define them within the broad environmental and geographic ecoregion conditions. These groupings can provide a structured framework for examining and comparing the diversity of life in freshwater systems. Covering virtually all freshwater habitats on Earth, this ecoregion map, together with associated species data, is a useful tool for underpinning global and regional conservation planning efforts, particularly to identify outstanding and imperiled freshwater systems; for serving as a logical framework for large-scale conservation strategies; and for providing a global-scale knowledge base for increasing freshwater biogeographic literacy. This version of the FEOW, modified by The Nature Conservancy, includes additional tabular data describing MHTs (similar to terrestrial biomes). The freshwater ecoregion map encompasses 426 units, whose boundaries generally, though not always, correspond with those of watersheds (also known as drainage basins or catchments). Within individual ecoregions there will be turnover of species, such as when moving up or down a river system, but taken as a whole an ecoregion will typically have a distinct evolutionary history and/or ecological processes. ### Overview The Global Peace Index (GPI) is a quantification of the absence of violence or the fear of violence to assess a nation’s level of peace. This lack of violence is defined as Negative Peace. A higher GPI represents a higher level of violence in a country. The Global Peace Index dataset was created by the Institute for Economics & Peace to measure global peacefulness. Its goal is to create understanding on the effects of violence and help countries develop the means to create peaceful societies. It measures a country’s level of Negative Peace using three domains of peacefulness: 1. *The extent of Ongoing Domestic and International Conflict:* This investigates the extent to which countries are involved in internal and external conflicts, as well as their role and duration of involvement in conflicts. This is based on six indicators, such as the number and duration of internal conflicts, number of deaths from external organized conflicts, and relationships with neighboring countries. 2. *The level of Societal Safety and Security:* It evaluates the level of harmony or discord within a nation using ten indicators. These indicators include topics like the level of perceived criminality in society, impact of terrorism, and political instability. 3. *The degree of Militarisation:* Militarisation refers to a country’s military build-up and access to weapons. This is determined by using seven indicators, such as military expenditure as a percentage of GDP, number of armed services personnel per 100,000 people, and nuclear and heavy weapons capabilities. The GPI data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available from 2008 to 2019 for 163 countries or independent territories covering 99.7% of the world’s population. This data can help to understand the economic value and trends of peace, and how to develop peaceful societies. ### Methodology The Global Peace Index uses 23 indicators in three domains to quantify the absence of violence or fear of violence. An international panel of independent experts helped to select the indicators in 2007 and reviews them on an annual basis. These 23 indicators were weighted and combined into two categories to create an overall score for GPI out of 100. The total GPI score was then simplified into a value of 1-5, with 5 being the highest amount of violence or fear being present within a country. The two overarching categories were a measure of how peaceful a country is internally and a measure of how peaceful a country is externally. The value of these two categories out of the total GPI value was 40% for external peace and 60% for internal peace. The weighting scheme was selected based on the relative importance of each indicator to achieve global peace. All scores for each indicator were normalized on a scale of 1-5. Qualitative indicators were banded into five groupings relevant to the indicator. Quantitative indicators were scored continuously based on relevant data and rounded to the third decimal point. The Economist Intelligence Unit’s team of country analysts scored seven of the eight qualitative indicators and also provided estimates about the gaps in the quantitative data. Scoring for qualitative indicators followed a strict set of guidelines to ensure reliability between values. Quantitative values were taken from a variety of international and government organizations. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://visionofhumanity.org/app/uploads/2019/07/GPI-2019web.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Chemicals and toxic pollutants in the environment affect millions of people each year in low- and middle-income countries. Without proper containment or public health interventions, these pollutants pose long-term problems to both the environment and people living in contaminated communities. The Toxic Sites Identification Program (TSIP) works to locate and assess contaminated sites in low- and middle-income countries and identify those that pose the greatest threat to human health. Coordinated by Pure Earth (formerly known as Blacksmith Institute) and funded by the European Commission, UNIDO, the World Bank Group, Green Cross Switzerland and others, the program has trained more than 400 investigators in nearly 50 countries. Investigators assess contaminated sites, undertake environmental sampling and collect health data using a rapid assessment tool called the Initial Site Screening (ISS) protocol. This protocol was developed based on US EPA protocols with the input and advice of experts from US EPA, Johns Hopkins School of Public Health and others. TSIP projects include reviews with local governments, NGOs, community groups, businesses and other stakeholders. Only sites that have exposures that exceed local or international standards for safety AND that demonstrate a credible pathway of exposure to a local population are included in the database. The database is uploaded monthly. More information on the TSIP database is available at the Learn More Link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview This dataset tracks the number of people who have been internally displaced due to conflict worldwide each year. Internal displacement refers to the forced movement of people within the country they live in. Millions of people are forced to flee their homes each year due to conflict, violence, development projects, disasters, and climate change and remain displaced within their countries of residence. Internally displaced persons (IDPs) can include both citizens and other habitual residents of the country, such as stateless persons. IDPs from conflict can include, but are not limited to - families caught between warring parties who had to flee their homes due to continuous attacks or threats; and - families pushed to leave their homes by constant harassment by local criminal gangs. Some of the typical needs and protection risks that arise in internal displacement include family separation, loss of documentation, loss of property, and further exposure to the risk of continued displacement. This dataset is produced by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) with the aim of informing policy and operational decisions in order to reduce the risk of future displacement and improve the lives of IDPs worldwide. Resource Watch also shows IDMC estimates of the number of people displaced annually due to [natural disasters](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522ef9945f7-d934-4a88-a02a-570f14fffefc%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25223bda62f1-7146-4dd5-bf3f-d3bfae26d0d7%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062a) at the national level, as well as [recent internal displacement from conflict, natural disasters, and development](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522d2f6245d-5b9b-4508-874b-d42a2be7d058%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25222059a368-b4f1-4c30-b874-b41e49c3c5e4%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062c), which are monitored in near real-time and displayed on an event-by-event basis. ### Methodology After IDMC learns that displacement due to conflict has occurred, it conducts situational monitoring within certain countries. At the end of the year, it reports the total number of people displaced in each country. For each event, information from a wide variety of different sources is compiled, generating the most comprehensive and reliable displacement estimate. These sources include national and subnational government authorities, UN agencies and other international organizations, related global databases, civil society organizations, news media outlets, and other entities. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.internal-displacement.org/database/methodology). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The UN Development Programme (UNDP) compiles the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) as part of its Human Development Report initiative. First published in 2010, the MPI identifies multiple deprivations at the household level in health, education, and standard of living. It uses microdata from household surveys, and—unlike the Inequality-Adjusted Human Development Index—all the indicators needed to construct the measure must come from the same survey. Each person in a given household is classified as poor or nonpoor depending on the weighted number of deprivations his or her household experiences. These data are then aggregated into the national measure of poverty. The MPI reflects both the prevalence of multidimensional deprivation and its intensity—the percentage of simultaneous deprivations poor people experience. It can be used to create a comprehensive picture of people living in poverty and permits comparisons both across countries, regions, and the world and within countries by ethnic group, urban, or rural location, as well as other key household and community characteristics. The MPI offers a valuable complement to income-based poverty measures. Indicators shown in the MPI include the following: (1) health: nutrition and child mortality; (2) education: years of schooling and children enrolled; and (3) standard of living: cooking fuel, sanitation, drinking water, electricity, housing, and assets. The MPI is calculated by multiplying the incidence of poverty by the intensity of poverty. The incidence of poverty is the proportion of people considered to experience multidimensional poverty, in other words, that are considered deprived in at least one-third of the MPI's weighted indicators. The intensity of multidimensional poverty is the weighted average number of deprivations poor people experience at the same time. The main data sources of the MPI are the Macro Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) of the Inner City Fund (ICF) and the Multiple Indicators Cluster Survey (MICS) of the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF). The 2020 Human Development Report (HDR) presents estimates for 107 countries—28 low income, 76 middle income, and 3 high income—and 5.9 billion people in developing regions. About 1.3 billion people in the 107 developing countries covered—22% of their entire population—lived in multidimensional poverty. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. ### Overview This dataset tracks the number of people who have been internally displaced due to natural disasters worldwide each year. “Internal displacement” refers to the forced movement of people within the country that they live in. Millions of people are forced to flee their homes each year due to conflict, violence, development projects, disasters, and climate change and remain displaced within their countries of residence. Internally displaced persons (IDPs) can include both citizens and other habitual residents of the country, such as stateless persons. IDPs from natural disasters may have been displaced by the following types of events: - Geophysical - earthquakes, mass movements, volcanic activity - Meteorological - storms, extreme temperatures - Hydrological - flooding, landslides, wave action - Climatological - wildfires Some of the typical needs and protection risks that arise in internal displacement include family separation, loss of documentation, loss of property, and further exposure to the risk of continued displacement. This dataset is produced by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) with the aim of informing policy and operational decisions in order to reduce the risk of future displacement and improve the lives of IDPs worldwide. Resource Watch also shows IDMC estimates of the number of people displaced annually due to [conflict](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%25226974833b-004e-4b24-bdbc-ffbb779c1496%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%2522cb5daeb3-80ef-4e6e-8ca8-5ed0d6170b3b%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=most-viewed&sortDirection=-1) at the national level, as well as [recent internal displacement from conflict, natural disasters, and development](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522d2f6245d-5b9b-4508-874b-d42a2be7d058%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25222059a368-b4f1-4c30-b874-b41e49c3c5e4%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062c), which are monitored in near real-time and displayed on an event-by-event basis. ### Methodology lDMC monitors displacements due to natural disasters on an event-by-event basis. At the end of the year, it reports the total number of people who were displaced in each country. For each event, information from a wide variety of different sources is compiled, generating the most comprehensive and reliable displacement estimate. These sources include national and subnational government authorities, UN agencies and other international organizations, related global databases, civil society organizations, news media outlets, and other entities. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.internal-displacement.org/database/methodology). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: ### Overview The Positive Peace Index (PPI) is a quantitative approach to measure Positive Peace. Positive Peace is defined as the attitudes, institutions, and structures that lead to a more peaceful society. A country with a higher PPI is more capable of building and maintaining peace. The Positive Peace Index dataset was created by the Institute for Economics & Peace to measure a country’s success in building and maintaining peace. Positive peace is used to create resilient and adaptive communities that prevent conflict and help societies channel disagreements productively. The framework for PPI is based on eight domains: 1. *Acceptance of the Rights of Others:* This requires countries to have formal laws that can guarantee basic human rights and freedoms, ensure gender equality, and worker’s rights. 2. *Equitable Distribution of Resources:* This ensures everyone has equal access to resources, such as education and health. 3. *Free Flow of Information:* This is measured by the extent to which citizens can gain access to information, whether the media is free and independent, and how well-informed citizens are. 4. *Good Relations with Neighbours:* A country’s relationship with other countries is an important indicator of how peaceful and politically stable the country is. 5. *High Levels of Human Capital:* The employment rate among young citizens and the number of people engaged in research activities shows the level of social capital in a country. 6. *Low Levels of Corruption:* High levels of corruption leads to a shortage of funding for essential services, which creates unrest in a society. 7. *Sound Business Environment:* This is measured by the presence of regulatory systems and formal institutions in a country to support a good business environment. 8. *Well-Functioning Government:* A government that delivers high-quality public and civil services, creates trust and participation, maintains political stability, and promotes the rule of law is necessary for a peaceful country. The PPI data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available from 2009 to 2018 for 163 countries covering 99.6% of the world’s population. This data can help to understand and make progress towards global peacefulness along with other interrelated areas such as: improved economic productivity and social advancement. ### Methodology The Positive Peace Index (PPI) uses 24 indicators in eight domains to measure Positive Peace. The eight domains range from the flow of information within a country to levels of corruption. PPI is interconnected to the Global Peace Index (GPI) which is another measurement for global peacefulness. GPI is a quantification of the absence of violence or the fear of violence in a country. The internal measures of the Global Peace Index were statistically compared to approximately 25,000 national data series, indices, and attitudinal surveys to determine the initial set of indicators for Positive Peace Index. These indicators were then qualitatively assessed. If there were multiple indicators for similar cases, the least important ones were discarded. Finally, the remaining indicators were aggregated into the eight domains of Positive Peace and given a correlation coefficient to their value in GPI using statistical approaches. The correlation coefficient represented how important the indicators were in the PPI measurement compared to GPI. The correlation coefficient was used to weight GPI Internal Peace scores for each indicator and create a final score out of 5. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://visionofhumanity.org/app/uploads/2019/10/PPR-2019-web.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/soc_092_positive_peace_index). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity, and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data covers select regions from East, West, and Central Africa, Central America, and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

### Overview The Cruise Ports dataset shows the number of visitors received by ports worldwide from July 2009 - June 2010. This dataset is part of the [Reefs at Risk Revisited](https://www.wri.org/publication/reefs-risk-revisited) report from World Resources Institute (WRI). Cruise port and passenger volume data was provided to WRI by [Clean Cruising](https://www.cleancruising.com.au/), a commercial cruise booking company based in Brisbane, Australia. Cruise ships can be a significant source of air and water pollution. According to a 2010 report from [Cruise Lines International Association](https://cruising.org/en/), a typical one-week cruise on a large ship (3,000 passengers and crew) generates almost 800 cubic meters of sewage; 3,700 cubic meters of graywater; half a cubic meter of hazardous waste; 8 tons of solid waste; and nearly 100 cubic meters of oily bilge water. Pollution from cruise ships can threaten coral reef health, particularly in the Atlantic where there are a large number of cruise ship ports. Cruise ships also produce harmful greenhouse gas emissions and can disturb marine wildlife. These problems are exacerbated in ports where several ships are frequently docked. Identifying locations and volume of cruise ship passengers can provide insight on where to expect environmental impacts to water and air quality at ports. The Cruise Ports dataset can also help inform environmental policy decisions in areas that receive high volumes of cruise ship passengers. The Cruise Ports dataset was provided by [WRI](https://www.wri.org/about), an independent, non-governmental global research organization that seeks to create equity and prosperity through sustainable natural resource management. WRI was founded in 1982 to address the environmental issues of deforestation, desertification and climate change. They use a science and evidence-based approach to achieve global change. WRI conducts independent research, tests ideas with leaders of cities, companies and countries, and implements proven ideas to transform societies and economies. ### Methodology The Cruise Ports dataset was generated by cruise port and passenger volume data provided by Clean Cruising. Passenger volume data was compiled from booking and departure information for all major cruise lines between July 2009 - June 2010. Port locations were mapped using the [National Geospatial Intelligence Agency World Port Index](https://msi.nga.mil/Publications/WPI.0). The Cruise Ports dataset was part of the Reefs at Risk Revisited report from WRI. For the full documentation, please see the source [technical documentation](https://www.wri.org/publication/reefs-risk-revisited). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Oil Pipelines data set was assembled by Professor Jeff Blossom of Harvard University's Center for Geographic Analysis for a workshop in 2009. It gives a partial view of installed crude oil, natural gas, and petroleum product pipeline infrastructure as of August 2009. It covers the entire globe. The lines may not exactly match up with actual pipeline coordinates in some areas, as there was uncertainty in the source maps. Pipelines are snapped to source cities, and the paths between cities are slightly stylized while maintaining the general trend of each pipeline's path. Esri's ArcGIS tool was used to georeference pipeline data from Theodora.com's pipeline maps: http://www.theodora.com/pipelines/. These maps were in turn assembled from a variety of different sources. According to the Theodora site, no claims are made regarding the accuracy of the world pipelines data. Not all pipelines contained in Theodora maps were transferred to this map. ### Overview The Gender Gap Index quantifies the gaps between women and men in four key areas: health, education, economy, and politics. Data is available from 149 countries for select years between 2010-2021. Scores are based on the level of access women have to resources and opportunities relative to men. Countries are given a score from 0-1. A score of 1 indicates full equality between women and men and a score of 0 indicates full inequality. The Gender Gap Index is published annually by the World Economic Forum (WEF) and is designed to capture the magnitude of gender-based disparities and track progress over time. Gender equality is a necessity for a peaceful, prosperous and sustainable world. Women represent half of the world’s population but continue to be underrepresented in leadership and in the workplace. According to the 2021 Gender Gap Index, only 27% of global managerial positions were held by women in 2021. The largest gap between women and men was in political empowerment, where only 26.1% of about 35,500 parliament seats and 22.6% of over 3,400 ministers globally are held by women. The Gender Gap Index serves as a benchmark for comparing countries and their progress to gender equality over time. Based on current trends, the WEF estimates that it will take 135.6 years to close the global gender gap. However, the 2021 Gender Gap Index shows that many countries have made significant progress towards closing the gender gap. These countries include Iceland, Finland, Norway, New Zealand, Sweden, Namibia, Rwanda, and Lithuania. The WEF Centre for the New Economy and Society published the Gender Gap Index. The WEF is an international NGO founded in 1971. Focused on public-private cooperation, the WEF brings together political, business and cultural leaders at their annual meetings, workshops and seminars. The WEF’s primary aim is to drive positive change for the world by conducting research, producing data and leading collaborative projects and initiatives. The Centre for the New Economy and Society is focused on closing economic gender gaps, fostering diversity and promoting inclusive growth. ### Methodology The Gender Gap Index quantified the gaps between men and women across four subindexes: economic participation and opportunity, educational attainment, health and survival, and political empowerment. Indicators were scored within each subindex. The Gender Gap Index was based on three underlying concepts that determined how indicators were chosen, how the data was treated and how the index can be used. These concepts can be thought of as the “rules” for how the subindexes were scored. First, the index measured gender-based gaps in access to resources and opportunities in countries, rather than the actual levels of the available resources and opportunities. This rewarded countries with smaller gaps in access to these resources, regardless of the overall level of resources. Second, the index evaluated countries based on outcomes rather than inputs. Inputs – indicators related to country-specific policies, rights or customs – were not included in the index. For example, the gap between women and men in high-skilled jobs (an outcome indicator) was measured, but the length of maternity leave (a country-specific policy) was not. Third, the index evaluated countries based on their proximity to gender equality, rather than their level of women’s empowerment. The index rewarded countries in which outcomes for women equaled those for men, but it neither rewarded nor penalized countries in which women outperformed men. The four subindexes were scored based on the following indicators: - Economic participation and opportunity: This subindex measured gender-based gaps in workforce participation, remuneration and advancement. The remuneration gap was measured by the ratio of estimated female-to-male earned income and a qualitative assessment of wage equality for similar work. The advancement gap was captured through two hard data statistics: the ratio of women to men among legislators, senior officials and managers, and the ratio of women to men among technical and professional workers. Data was provided by the [International Labour Organization ILOSTAT database](https://ilostat.ilo.org/) and the WEF. - Educational attainment: Gender-based gaps in educational attainment were measured with the ratio of women to men enrolled in primary, secondary and tertiary education. The ratio of female to male literacy was also used as an indicator of a country’s long-term ability to educate women and men. Data was provided by the [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Institute for Statistics Education Indicators database](http://uis.unesco.org/). - Health and survival: The differences between women’s and men’s health were measured using the sex ratio at birth and the gap between women’s and men’s healthy life expectancy. Sex ratio at birth is the measure of male births for every female birth and was included to capture the phenomenon of [“missing women.”](https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2015/10/where-are-all-the-women/) This refers to the observation of a low ratio of women to men, particularly in countries with a strong son preference. Data for this subindex was provided by the [United Nations (UN) World Population Prospects dataset](https://population.un.org/wpp/) and the [World Health Organization (WHO) Global Health Observatory database](https://www.who.int/data/gho). - Political empowerment: The gap between women and men at the highest level of political decision-making was measured by the ratio of women to men in ministerial positions and the ratio of women to men in parliamentary positions. The ratio of women to men in terms of years in executive office (prime minister or president) for the last 50 years was also included. Data was provided by the Inter-Parliamentary Union [Women in National Parliaments](http://archive.ipu.org/wmn-e/classif.htm). [Women in Politics](https://www.ipu.org/resources/publications/infographics/2020-03/women-in-politics-2020) datasets and the WEF. All data was converted to female-to-male ratios. Ratios were then truncated at the “equality benchmark”. The equality benchmark was 1 for all indicators except the two in the health subindex. The sex ratio at birth equality benchmark was 0.9445 and the healthy life expectancy benchmark was 1.06. Truncating ratios at 1 assigns the same score to a country that has reached equality between women and men (a ratio of 1) and one in which women have surpassed men (a ratio greater than 1). This method measured how close women were to achieving equality with men in a country, but did not reward or penalize countries with a gender gap in the opposite direction. The total score for each subindex was a weighted average of the scores for each indicator. A weighted average was used to make sure each indicator had the same relative impact on the total score.The overall score for each country was a simple average of the subindex scores. A score of 0 indicated complete inequality between women and men and a score of 1 indicated complete equality. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://reports.weforum.org/global-gender-gap-report-2018/measuring-the-global-gender-gap/). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. As one of the four indicators in the Natural Resource Management Index, NRPI shows the degree to which a country protects at least 17% of terrestrial biome within its borders. It is computed as a standardized proximity-to-target ranging from 0 (worst performance) to 100 (at target or best performance). Biomes are broad ecological regions (e.g., a desert or deciduous forest). CIESIN utilized the 2016 World Database of Protected Areas (WDPA), ISciences coastline data set, and WWF's Terrestrial Ecoregions of the World data set (Olson et al. 2001) to compute the proportion of each biome in a country that is protected. The WDPA includes polygons that provide the actual boundaries of protected areas. The biome data, provided by the WWF data set, are manually matched with ISciences coastline data to ensure that all areas, particularly along the coast or small islands, are assigned a biome type. A composite layer consisting of all three data sets was created and the percentage of each biome that is protected was calculated. The percentage was capped at 17%, so that additional "credit" does not accrue where protection exceeds 17%. The countries' overall scores are a weighted average of the protection score for each biome. The weights are derived by calculating the biome area as a fraction of a country’s overall land area. Greater weights are applied to larger biomes. The indicator covers 237 countries and is updated based on the most recent monthly release of UNEP's World Conservation Monitoring WDPA. For more information, please see http://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/set/nrmi-natural-resource-protection-child-health-indicators-2016/docs Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

### Overview The Distribution of Consumer Spending by Sector dataset estimates the share of household income that is spent on various types of products and services. Spending was analyzed for four consumption segments: lowest, low, middle, and higher. The four levels of consumption segments were based on income per capita: - Lowest: below $2.97 per capita a day - Low: between $2.97 and $8.44 per capita a day - Middle: between $8.44 and $23.03 per capita a day - Higher: above $23.03 per capita a day This dataset shows the percent of the household income that is spent on each type of product or service within each of these consumption segments. This dataset was developed by the World Bank Group as part of its Global Consumption Database. The data covers both urban and rural households in developing countries and is reported at the national level for the year 2010. ### Methodology The Distribution of Consumer Spending by Sector dataset was developed using multiple different surveys, depending on data availability, including household budget survey, living standard measurement surveys, and various kinds of country-specific socioeconomic surveys. All surveys measure consumption at the household level; however, different surveys collected data over different time periods. Some conducted surveys over a period of 12 months to account for seasonality, while others collected data over a shorter period (a few weeks or a few months). Most surveys rely on the "recall method," in which households are asked to report what they can recall spending over a given period. The choice of recall period may have a significant impact on the level of consumption reported by the households. Data was collected for households in various developing countries. These households were categorized by their consumption segments for the Global Consumption Database. The consumption segments are based on the global income distribution data, which rank the global population by income per capita. The lowest consumption segment corresponds to the bottom half of the global distribution, or the 50th percentile and below; the low consumption segment to the 51st-75th percentiles; the middle consumption segment to the 76th-90th percentiles; and the higher consumption segments to the 91st percentile and above. The purchasing power parity (PPP) US dollar threshold was converted into annual expenditure in local currency (as of 2010). The Global Consumption Database draws on a diverse array of data surveys, so standardization was applied, to the extent possible, through a six-step process. The first step consisted of annualizing each household's consumption or expenditure data for each commodity. The second step was to detect and fix outliers. The third step was to map commodities found in each survey dataset to a standard classification of products and services. In the fourth step, extrapolations were done to convert all consumption and population data to a common reference year. In the fifth and sixth step, the resulting data was compared with data from other sources and used to generate a standard set of tables for each country showing consumption and demographic patterns across consumption segments. With the goal of producing information for decadal-scale planning, adaptation, and investment, the Aqueduct Water Stress Projections model potential changes in future demand and supply of water over the next 3 decades. This data set displays the rates of literacy per enumeration area from the Seychelles National Bureau of Statistics 2010 Population and Housing Census Report. This report has been published 6 times: in 1977, 1987, 1994, 1997, 2002 and 2010. The next census is scheduled to be published in 2020. There are over 600 enumeration areas on the 3 main islands of Seychelles; this data set focuses on the enumeration areas on Mahé. Enumeration areas are composed of approximately 50-70 dwelling units each. The boundaries were drawn to make the workload for each field worker manageable, outline each area distinctly, ensure complete coverage, and avoid double-counting households. The literacy rates were calculated by dividing the number of literate individuals in an enumeration area by the population of the respective enumeration area and converted to a percentage. This data represents the percentage of the population in each enumeration area that is classified as literate.

### Overview This dataset shows a global estimate of plastic inputs from rivers into the oceans for 2010, expressed in kilograms per year. The authors used data on waste management, population density, and hydrological information to create this model. The dataset includes information on 40,760 watersheds and 182 different countries. The data is presented in a vector format. Plastic pollution in our oceans and on our coastlines have become a major threat to ocean health worldwide. A better understanding and quantification of marine plastic sources can help in implementing mitigation strategies to alleviate the issue. The dataset can help in identifying places that require higher attention in terms of plastic waste monitoring and mitigation plans. This data can also be used as a baseline measurement for ocean plastic mass balance exercises. This data was developed by researchers funded by The Ocean Cleanup Foundation. ### Methodology The amount of plastic inputs from rivers into the oceans was estimated by using data on mismanaged plastic waste production (MPW) per country, population density, topographic elevation, and location of artificial barriers (weirs and dams). For each catchment area mismanaged plastic waste production (MPW) rates per day were calculated by combining data on waste generation by inhabitant per day and population density for the area. This data was combined with water flow per river catchment area to provide a final value for the mass of plastic released at the river’s mouth. This data was extrapolated using seasonal variations in water flow to create a year dataset. Data on population density was derived from the dataset Global 15 x 15 Minute Grids of the Downscaled Population by the Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (SEDAC) for 182 countries. Data used to calculate MPW rates were collected from seven peer reviewed studies. Topographic information was taken from Global Land Data Assimilation System (GLDAS) hydrological model for surface/subsurface runoff and location of artificial barriers was taken from AquaStat and Global Reservoir and Dam Database (GRanD). In total the dataset includes information for 40,760 watersheds worldwide. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology]( https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms15611#Sec6). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for plastic input in tonnes per year, plastic input in tonnes per month, and average monthly water runoff in catchment area in mm per day are also available from the data provider. ### Overview The Crop Land and Production dataset shows the global harvested area, production, and yield for six major crops: wheat, soybean, rice, maize, coffee, and cotton. The dataset was derived from the 2010 Spatial Production Allocation Model (SPAM). The SPAM model aimed to disaggregate (downscale) national and sub-national crop statistics using a variety of inputs, such as cropland surface, location of irrigated areas, crop suitability and potential yields, rural population densities, production systems characteristics and crop prices. Crop data was downscaled to a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes. This spatial resolution is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels, and increased biofuel demand. Increased demand for these resources will significantly affect land and resource use, climate change, political agendas, and technological developments. A comprehensive understanding of the current spatial distribution of the world’s crops is necessary in order to preemptively address these effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset can be used to understand the extent and productivity of key global crops, which will help address food crop demand and its effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was generated by the [Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research Program on Policies, Institutions, and Markets (CGIAR-PIM)](https://pim.cgiar.org/about/). CGIAR-PIM provides support for policies that help farmers improve their lives, produce nutritious and affordable foods, and protect the soil, water and biodiversity in rural landscapes. The program is led by the [International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI)](https://www.ifpri.org/about), a CGIAR-PIM research center. IFPRI provides research-based policy solutions to sustainably reduce poverty and end hunger in developing countries. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was part of the larger SPAM dataset, which was developed for the HarvestChoice research initiative. Conducted by IFPRI, [HarvestChoice](https://www.ifpri.org/project/harvestchoice) generated knowledge products to help guide strategic investments to improve the well-being of poor people in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia through more productive and profitable farming. ### Methodology The main purpose of SPAM is to disaggregate crop statistics (e.g., harvested area, production quantity, and yield) by different farming systems and to further allocate such disaggregated statistics into spatially gridded units. The whole procedure entails a data fusion approach that combines information from different sources and at different spatial scales by deploying various matching and calibration processes. Then all the data elements are processed by the optimization model, which generates results at the grid level. There are three submodules in a standardized SPAM model: disaggregation, optimization, and allocation. The SPAM2010 is conceptualized based on this general setting, while it adds further methodological and data improvements, which mainly include the update of base year, the expansion of subnational administrative-unit coverage, the extension of crop list, and the substitution of the latest hybrid cropland map as the basic allocation layer. The first step for SPAM is to disaggregate crop statistics of agricultural production (e.g., the yield, harvested area, and total production) by administrative-unit levels (k), crop type (j), and farming system (l) from coarser scale to finer scale. The four production systems were defined by water and management type: - Irrigated – high input (I) - Rainfed – high input (H) - Rainfed – low input (L) - Rainfed – subsistence (S) The four conceptualized farming systems are mainly delineated by the water supply system and inputs used by farmers, despite global data on farming system shares for each crop being largely absent. For a small number of large countries, e.g., Brazil, China, India, Russia, the United States, the authors have data on farming system shares at the ADM1 level. For the other countries the authors assigned the national farming system shares to each ADM1 level and then adjusted individual ADM1 farming system shares in light of the supporting evidence. For irrigated farming systems, the crop-specific shares are derived by dividing the harvested area cultivated under full control irrigation obtained from [Global Information System on Water and Agriculture (AQUASTAT)](https://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/), [MIRCA](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2008GB003435), and country-level statistics by the overall harvested area. The optimization module in SPAM2010 is almost the same as that in previous versions. The authors applied a cross-entropy process in the General Algebraic Modeling System (GAMS), which ensures that the optimization procedure iterates until a solution is found. Once the allocation is successful, meaning that an optimal or locally optimal solution has been found, the routine immediately returns the allocated physical area by grid, crop and farming system, and the program continues with post-processing automatically. The SPAM model used additional biological and economic inputs to allocate the statistics within each pixel. Input data included (among several others): - Administrative units - Crop Type - Farming system - Adjusted harvested area - Total suitable area in each grid by crop and farming system - Crop prices - Market accessibility in each grid - Population density Our data catalog provides three of the SPAM2010 essential output indicators: - Harvested Area: also measured in hectares, harvested area is at least as large as physical area but sometimes more since it also accounts for multiple harvests of a crop on the same plot. Like for physical area, the harvested area is calculated for each production system, and the sum of all harvested areas of all production systems in a pixel amounts to the total harvested area of the pixel. The sum of all the harvested areas of the crops in a pixel can be larger than the pixel size. - Production: for each production system and crop, production is calculated by multiplying the area harvested by its corresponding yield. It is measured in metric tons. The total production of a crop includes the production of all production systems of that crop. - Yield: is the amount of production per harvested area and measured in kilograms per hectare. It is a measure of productivity. The total yield of a crop, when considering all production systems, is the weighted average of the four systems’ yields. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/12/3545/2020/essd-12-3545-2020.pdf). ### Additional Information Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. This map of baseline water stress in major crop producing areas was created by WRI's Aqueduct program as part of the Water Risk Atlas, an online mapping tool that displays various aspects of water-related risks. The map displays the major crop producing areas for 13 major commodity crops (cocoa, coffee, cotton, maize, oats, oil palm, oranges, canola, rice, rubber, soybeans, sugarcane, and wheat) and 9 crop groups (cereals, fiber crops, fodder crops, fruits, oil crops, legumes, roots and tubers, sugar crops, and tree nuts), and the levels of water stress (low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high) experienced in these major crop-producing areas. Baseline water stress refers to the annual water withdrawals (municipal, industrial, and agricultural) expressed as a percentage of the total annual available flow. Higher values indicate more competition among users. Arid areas with low water use are shown in gray but scored as high stress when calculating aggregated scores. Baseline water stress is calculated by dividing water withdrawals (2010) by mean available blue water (1950-2008). Areas with available blue water and water withdrawal less than 0.03 and 0.012/m2 respectively are coded as “arid and low water use." Crop production in each category is computed by overlaying gridded crop production data, which was pulled from 2 articles in Global Biogeochemical Cycle (2008), "Farming the Planet: 1. Geographic Distribution of Global Agricultural Lands in the Year 2000" and "Farming the Planet: 2. Geographic Distribution of Crop Areas, Yields, Physiological Types, and Net Primary Production in the Year 2000." The authors of these studies identified croplands and crop production using a high-resolution satellite-derived land cover data set and agricultural inventory data to derive a global map of croplands. PREPdata shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

We recommend using [this dataset](c66d7f3a-d1a8-488f-af8b-302b0f2c3840) as a replacement.**_ In response to growing concerns from private sector actors around water availability, water quality, climate change, and increasing demand, World Resources Institute developed Aqueduct Global Maps to help decision-makers identify areas with higher exposure to water-related risks. Aqueduct employs the composite index approach as a robust communication tool to translate hydrological data into intuitive indicators of water-related risks. 12 indicators were grouped into a framework identifying spatial variation in water risks for 15,006 subcatchments. The 12 global indicators (baseline water stress, interannual variability, seasonal variability, flood occurrence, drought severity, upstream storage, groundwater stress, return flow ratio, upstream protected land, media coverage, access to water, and threatened amphibians) were grouped into 3 categories of risk (physical quantity, quality, and regulatory and reputational risk) and 1 overall score. For 6 of the 12 indicators, an ensemble of time series estimators, spatial regression, and a sparse hydrological model was used to generate novel data sets of water supply and use. The remaining 6 indicators were adapted from existing publications. Aggregation methods were chosen to maximize transparency and communicability, and to allow for dynamic weighting to reflect different users’ sensitivities to water-related risks. Catchments with less than 0.012 m/m²/year of withdrawal and 0.03 m/m²/year of available blue water were masked out as “arid and low water use.” Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. The Gridded Livestock of the World Version 3, produced by the Food and Agriculture Organization and the University of Oxford, shows the distribution of eight livestock animal densities in animals per square kilometer at a spatial resolution of 5 arcminutes. The animals include cattle, water buffalo, horse, sheep, goats, pigs, chickens and ducks. The Gridded Livestock of the World (GLW) created two versions of their data for two different methods of distributing livestock census weighting: area weighting and dasymetric weighting. Resource Watch displays the dasymetric weighting data, and the metadata refers to this methodology. More information can be found in the Cautions section. The total livestock census numbers for administrated levels are found by mining agricultural yearbooks or through direct contacts with ministries or statistical bureau. The livestock numbers are then distributed within census polygons according to weights established by a Random Forest model using high resolution spatial covariates including population, vegetation health, and climate. In compiling subnational census counts, priority is given to censuses that most closely match the reference year, 2010, and those with the highest level of spatial detail. This results in a global mosaic of data from different spatial resolutions and different years. Both the spatial resolution and year of census data depend on the country and species in question. See cautions section and source publication for more information. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. ### Overview The Oil Palm Concessions dataset shows public lands allocated by governments to private companies for industrial-scale oil palm plantations. The dataset is a compilation of concession data from Cameroon, Indonesia, Liberia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Republic of the Congo and the Solomon Islands. Concession name, company and area in hectares (ha) are included in the Oil Palm Concessions dataset. Oil Palm Concessions data is typically from government agencies or nonprofits, although the data source and date vary by country. The Oil Palm Concessions dataset is updated monthly. Palm oil is an edible vegetable oil produced from the fruits of the oil palm tree. According to the [World Wildlife Fund (WWF)](https://www.worldwildlife.org/industries/palm-oil), oil palm is a highly productive crop and grows only in tropical regions. Palm oil does not require refrigeration and is used in food products, cosmetics and detergents. However, oil palm farming contributes to deforestation and the release of harmful greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. [According to a study from the European Commission](http://pure.iiasa.ac.at/id/eprint/14868/), oil palm farming is responsible for 8% of global agriculture-related deforestation. Deforestation from oil palm farming is most prevalent in Indonesia, Brazil and Malaysia. Deforestation has many harmful impacts on the environment, including habitat destruction, erosion, air pollution and groundwater contamination. Understanding the locations and extent of oil palm plantations provides information about potential environmental impacts. It can also be used to encourage farmers and businesses to use sustainable farming practices. The Oil Palm Concessions dataset was generated by [Global Forest Watch (GFW)](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/about/), an organization established in 1997 by the [World Resources Institute](https://www.wri.org/). WRI is an independent, non-governmental global research organization which seeks to create equity and prosperity through sustainable natural resource management. They provide data and research about climate, energy, food, forests, water, cities and oceans. GFW uses satellite data and cloud computing to monitor deforestation in near real-time. This information is critical to ending illegal deforestation and fires, and promoting sustainable practices. It can be used by business owners and the public to monitor the environmental impacts of activities like logging, mining and farming. Additionally, farmers and landowners can use this data to protect their land and resources. ### Methodology The term “oil palm concession” refers to an area allocated by a government to a company for industrial-scale oil palm plantations. GFW generated the Oil Palm Concessions dataset by compiling concession data from Cameroon, Indonesia, Liberia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Republic of the Congo and Solomon Islands. Most locations in the dataset include the company, concession name and concession area (ha). Data for each country was collected from various sources, including from government agencies and public documents. The most common source was maps from forestry or agriculture-specific government agencies. Data from the public domain (company websites, news reports, NGOs) was used for countries where data was not readily available from government agencies. This data was used to create polygons representing the locations and boundaries of concessions. Additional information such as company and concession name was added to the polygons as attributes. The Oil Palm Concessions dataset was published in 2019, though the exact dates vary by country. Concession data for each country is available on the [GFW Open Data Portal](https://data.globalforestwatch.org/search?q=oilpalm).
