description: ### Overview The Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources dataset shows the locations of the Assessment Units (AUs) in the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) World Assessment of Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources. The assessment was conducted in 2012 and evaluated 313 AUs within 171 geologic provinces (areas where oil and gas occur in commercial quantities). An AU is a mappable volume of rock with homogenous geologic properties. Each AU was assessed for undiscovered oil and gas resources using data from published literature. In each geologic province, total petroleum systems (TPS) were also defined. A TPS is the group of geologic elements needed for oil and gas formation. The Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources dataset provides an understanding of the quantity, quality and distribution of global conventional oil and gas resources. Conventional oil and gas resources, such as crude oil and natural gas, are found in high porosity/permeability reservoirs. Unconventional oil and gas resources are found in low porosity/permeability reservoirs, such as shale and tar sands. Conventional resources are relatively easy to extract from the earth and do not require fracking. The [USGS World Assessment of Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources](https://certmapper.cr.usgs.gov/data/apps/we-data/) determined that a total of 565,298 million barrels of oil, 5,605,626 billion cubic feet of gas and 166,668 million barrels of natural gas liquids remained undiscovered as of 2011. All of these resources are conventionally extractable. However, conventional oil and gas resources are dwindling. Knowing where and how much conventional oil and gas remains undiscovered is important for understanding the world’s energy future. The Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources dataset is a geologic basis for making decisions about energy. It can help predict future energy production trends and increase understanding of the social and environmental consequences of oil and gas resource exploitation. Established in 1879, the [USGS](https://www.usgs.gov/) is a scientific organization within the U.S. Department of the Interior. The USGS’s purpose is to collect, monitor, analyze and provide science about natural resource conditions and issues. The Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources dataset was generated from data published by the [USGS Central Energy Resource Science Center (CERSC)](https://www.usgs.gov/centers/cersc), a group that conducts interdisciplinary research on global geoscience and energy systems. The CERSC studies the geological processes critical to the formation of natural resources. They also evaluate the environmental and socioeconomic effects of the production and usage of oil and gas resources. ### Methodology The Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources dataset shows the locations of areas assessed in the 2012 USGS World Assessment of Undiscovered Oil and Gas Resources. Data is available for the entire world, excluding the U.S. The study evaluated 313 AUs within 171 geologic provinces. Geologic provinces are areas that encompass a natural geologic setting, such as a sedimentary basin or delta, and are contiguous for hundreds to thousands of kilometers. Geologic provinces contain valuable quantities of oil and gas resources. Each province contains at least one TPS. A TPS are areas that contain all the necessary essential geologic elements and processes required for oil and gas to form. The geologic elements are source rock, reservoir, seal and overburden. In each province, these elements were mapped, described and modeled based on data from published literature. The data source provides [a viewer](https://certmapper.cr.usgs.gov/data/apps/world-energy/?resource=conventional) where you can select an AU and reference the published literature. AUs were defined within each TPS. A TPS typically contains only one AU, although some TPSs were divided into more than one AU. An AU is a homogeneous package of rock that contains oil and gas resources from a single TPS. Any given AU has the same set of geologic processes that led to the generation, migration and storage of oil and gas. All AUs were analyzed to determine their quantities of undiscovered, technically recoverable oil and gas resources. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://pubs.usgs.gov/fs/2012/3042/). ### Additional Information Approximately 75% of the undiscovered oil and gas resources are in the following four regions: South America and the Caribbean, sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and North Africa, and the Arctic regions of North America. The full assessment and data for each AU is available [here](https://certmapper.cr.usgs.gov/data/apps/world-energy/?resource=conventional). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

Crude Rate of Emergency Department Visits for Asthma per 10,000 Population data set contains case counts of asthma emergency department (ED) visits using admission date among residents of the United States. It includes emergency department visits during a calendar year with asthma as the primary diagnosis (including records for emergency department visits resulting in a hospitalization.) These data are stratified by year of admission, county (only for Asthma), state, and gender. Annual Crude rates are calculated using Midyear and postcensal resident population, by age and sex, for state and county. Age-adjusted rates are calculated by method to Year 2000 US Standard Population. ED visits data were submitted by 25 states and 1 city: California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, New York City, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Utah, Vermont, Washington, and Wisconsin. CDC Tracking Network suppresses data for counties with non-zero counts less than 6 and population less than 100,000 to protect confidentiality. These measures can be used to assess the burden of Asthma, monitor trends over time, identify high-risk groups, and enhance prevention, education, and evaluation efforts. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

This data set of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) attributable to the environment, adjusted for differences in the age distribution of populations and expressed in a percentage impact per 100,000 population, represents the burden of disease that could be avoided by modifying the environment. Modifiable environment includes (1) air, soil, and water pollution with chemicals or biological agents, (2) ultraviolet and ionizing radiation, (3) built environment, (4) noise and electromagnetic fields, (5) occupational risks, (6) agricultural methods and irrigation schemes, (7) anthropogenic climate changes and ecosystem degradation, and (8) individual behaviors related to the environment; such as hand-washing and food contamination with unsafe water or dirty hands. The results are based on a combination of (1) comparative risk assessments, (2) calculations based on more limited epidemiological data, (3) entire attribution of certain diseases to the environment based on their transmission pathway, and (4) surveys of expert opinions on the attributable fractions for some environmental risks. Attributable fractions were estimated for 92 of the 133 major diseases and injuries quantified by WHO. The figures represent the sum of all the attributable DALYs. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) active fires data (VNP14IMGT) constitute the latest fire monitoring product to be added to FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System), which identifies global fire locations in near-real time. Information is collected from the VIIRS sensor and processed with a fire detection algorithm to flag active fires. Each dot on the map represents the center of a 375 m pixel that has been flagged by the algorithm. The VIIRS data provides a higher resolution data set than the active fires data from MODIS. The VIIRS data have higher spatial resolution (375 m pixels vs. 1 km pixels), which improves detection of smaller fires and provides a more reliable estimate of fire perimeters. The VIIRS data are also better calibrated to detect fires at night. The active fires data are available to view and download for the past 24 hours, 48 hours, or 7 days. Older fire data will be available for download from the NASA FIRMS website beginning in mid-2016. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspot /fire pixels. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

### Overview This dataset includes near-real-time active fires as points that represent the center of a 375 m resolution pixel and is being updated twice daily. The data is collected from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) sensor on Suomi-National Polar-Orbiting Partnership (Suomi-NPP) satellite. This dataset is provided through the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) Fire Email Alerts. This dataset provides improved response for smaller fires, mapping of large fire perimeters, and better detection at night, when fire activities usually occur. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of detection. This dataset is well suited for use in near-real time alert systems, fire tracking, and management. ### Methodology Fire detections are determined using a multispectral contextual algorithm to identify subpixel fire activity and other thermal anomalies in the Level 1 (swath) input data. The algorithm uses all five 375 m VIIRS channels to detect fires and separate land, water, and cloud pixels in the image. Fire locations are then given as the center of a 375 m pixel that has been flagged by the algorithm. The algorithm first screens for cloud and water pixels. Next potential fires are found using criteria based on brightness detected by the channels. These fires are then filtered by the algorithm to find the distinct radiometric signatures associated with active fires. Finally custom filters are applied to reduce false alarm rates. False alarms usually come from areas of high solar reflection such as metallic rooftops in industrial parks or bright surfaces such as concrete pavement. Confidence values are available for each fire detection. They are based on a collection of intermediate algorithm quantities used in the detection process and are intended to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspot/fire pixels. Confidence values are set to low, nominal, and high. Low confidence daytime fire pixels are typically associated with areas of sun glint and lower relative temperature anomaly (<15K) in the mid-infrared channel I4. Nominal confidence pixels are those free of potential sun glint contamination during the day and marked by strong (>15K) temperature anomaly in either day or nighttime data. High confidence fire pixels are associated with day or nighttime saturated pixels. For the full documentation of the initial algorithm methodology, please see the source [methodology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0034425713004483). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Resource Watch displays the most recent fires in the past week. Data older than the last seven days or within the temporal coverage of January 20, 2012, to the present is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map this data for display on Resource Watch. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

### Overview The Apparent Fishing Effort dataset, produced by Global Fishing Watch (GFW), shows the distribution of time spent fishing in different locations throughout the ocean at a 0.01 degree resolution between 2012 and 2021. The time spent fishing in each pixel is tracked using a maritime Automatic Identification System (AIS). Commercial fishing is a vital part of the global economy and is crucial to the food security and cultural identity of millions of people. However some practices, like trawling and dredging, destroy far more ocean habitat than any other fishing practice. When dredging or trawling, commercial vessels drag a dredge or heavy net, respectively, along the seafloor to scrape up species like oysters or shrimp. The process of scraping the seafloor is extremely destructive to deep-sea marine ecosystems, productivity, biodiversity, and carbon storage. Historically, practices like trawling and dredging have been difficult and costly to monitor, but technology and transparency are driving tangible change in how the sector is managed. Global Fishing Watch is advancing ocean governance through increased transparency of human activity at sea. By creating and publicly sharing map visualizations, data and analysis tools, they enable scientific research and drive a transformation in how we manage our ocean. By 2030, they aim to monitor and visualize the impact of ocean-going vessels, both industrial and small-scale, that are responsible for the vast majority of the global seafood catch. ### Methodology Global Fishing Watch’s apparent fishing effort dataset is based on transmissions broadcast using publicly available automatic identification system (AIS) information. AIS is a GPS-like device that large ships use to broadcast their position in order to avoid collisions. Each year, more than 400,000 AIS devices broadcast vessel location along with other information on vessel identity, course and speed. Ground stations and satellites pick up this information, meaning a ship’s movements can be followed even in the most remote parts of the ocean. GFW uses two convolutional neural networks (CNN)—a cutting edge form of machine learning model—to help classify fishing vessels (vessel characterization model) and predict when they are fishing (fishing detection model). They first [identify fishing vessels](https://globalfishingwatch.org/datasets-and-code-vessel-identity/) by combining a comprehensive database of vessel registry information with the output of the vessel characterization model to predict features like geartype and size. Next, GFW estimates where and when each vessel is fishing based on its movement patterns. The fishing detection model was trained using over a thousand manually labeled vessel tracks to learn what fishing movements look like. This model predicts a score for every AIS position in the database to distinguish fishing positions from non-fishing positions, such as during vessel transits. When the fishing detection model scores an AIS position as a fishing position, the time associated with that AIS position is considered apparent fishing activity. For more information about the two models, please see the supplementary materials of the [associated paper](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aao5646). After identifying fishing vessels and detecting fishing positions in the AIS data, apparent fishing effort can be calculated for any area by summarizing the fishing hours for all fishing vessels in that area. Global Fishing Watch’s fishing detection algorithm is a best effort mathematically to identify “apparent fishing activity.” As a result, it is possible that some fishing activity is not identified as such by Global Fishing Watch; conversely, Global Fishing Watch may show apparent fishing activity where fishing is not actually taking place. To generate maps of apparent fishing effort GFW “rasterizes” the AIS positions by placing them into a grid and calculating the total fishing activity in each grid cell. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aao5646) ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. This map displays effort by trawlers or dredgers. Resource Watch shows separate GFW fishing effort data [for all other vessels](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/11f16cb9-def0-4bd5-a60e-50c542b837e3). [Data disaggregated by flag state, vessel, and gear type](https://globalfishingwatch.org/data-download/datasets/public-fishing-effort) is also available through Global Fishing Watch. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team requested a visualization of the data through the Global Fishing Watch API. This visualization powered by 4-Wings, Global Fishing Watch experimental technology for rapid access to global scale temporal data sets. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github.](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/com_030c_rw1_trawling_activity) ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

description: FORMA alerts are processed in Google Earth Engine (GEE) using a combination of two MODIS products: NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index), and FIRMS (Fires Information for Resource Management System). NDVI updates are processed every 16 days, while fire updates are processed daily. Models are developed individually for each ecogroup to relate the two inputs to the area of clearing, using the Hansen annual tree cover loss data to train the model. The minimum threshold to qualify as an alert is 25% of the pixel cleared, though thresholds vary by ecogroup to minimize false positives. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

This data set includes layers showing water infrastructure in India, including large dams, powerhouses, and reservoirs. This data was generated under the India Water Resources Information System (India-WRIS) using Central Water Commission (CWC) and state water resources and irrigation datasets. The dams layer contains the locations of 4161 dams out of 5125 dams listed in National Register of Large Dams from the CWC. The powerhouses layer contains the locations of 304 powerhouses of India under hydroelctric projects. The reservoirs layer contains CWC monitoring reservoirs. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

The Crude Rate of Emergency Department Visits for Heat Stress per 100,000 Population data set contains case counts of heat stress illness emergency department (ED) visits using admission date among residents of the United States. These data are stratified by year of admission, state, and gender. Emergency department visit records are selected using primary and other diagnosis codes and emergency department visit date between May 1 and September 30 for each year. Annual Crude rates are calculated using Midyear and postcensal resident population, by age and sex, for state and county. Age-adjusted rates are calculated by method to Year 2000 US Standard Population. ED visits data were submitted by 25 states and 1 city: California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, New York City, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Utah, Vermont, Washington, and Wisconsin. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Tracking Network suppresses data for counties with non-zero counts less than 6 and population less than 100,000 to protect confidentiality. Increases in the rates of ED visits for heat stress are one potential impact of rising global temperatures. Tracking these data can help document changes over place and time, monitor vulnerable areas, and evaluate the results of local climate-adaptation strategies. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

The Ocean Health Index, developed by the National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis (NCEAS) at the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB), measures the global state of the world's oceans. By providing a tool for the ongoing assessment of ocean health, the index can inform policy decisions about how to use or protect marine ecosystems. The Ocean Health Index uses data from global databases to annually assess 221 regions, including all coastal countries, territories, and the Antarctic. The Index is comprised of ten overarching goals that represent the wide range of benefits a healthy ocean can provide: Food Provision, Artisanal Fishing Opportunities, Natural Products, Carbon Storage, Coastal Protection, Tourism & Recreation, Coastal Livelihoods & Economies, Sense of Place, Clean Waters, and Biodiversity. Four dimensions are measured and scored for each goal: status, trend, pressures, and resilience. Present status is a goal’s current value compared to its reference point. Trend is the average percent change of a goal’s status over the most recent five years. Pressures are the ecological and social factors that decrease status. Resilience includes the ecological factors and social initiatives (policies, laws, etc.) that increase status by reducing or eliminating pressures. Scores for the Trend, Pressures and Resilience dimensions are combined as Like Future Status, an indicator of what the status score is likely to be in five years. The Goal Score is the average of the scores for Present Status and Likely Future Status. Status (including Trend) thus makes up 83% of the goal score, while Pressures and Resilience each contribute 8.5%. A region's score, which ranges from 0-100, is the average of its goal scores. This data set was compiled from data derived from the National Bureau of Soil Survey and Land Use Planning (NBSS LUP) Soil Map under the Indian Farmers Fertiliser Cooperative Limited (IFFCO) project of the Regional Remote Sensing Centre West (RRSC-W) of the Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO). Data contains information about soil depth, erosion, slope, productivity and texture. Generated under India-WRIS using Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) datasets. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

The annual PM2.5 Level (Monitor Only) data set is provided by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and offers a general indication of the overall trend in annual PM2.5 concentrations. It can be used to inform policy makers and the public about the degree of potential exposures to fine particles within a state during a year and over time (trends), based on the annual National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) of 15 µg/m³ for PM2.5 developed by EPA. The annual average measures of PM2.5 are created using the site-level daily monitoring data. Only monitors that have at least 11 observations for each of the four calendar quarters are considered complete. The annual averages are computed only for monitors that satisfy the completeness criteria. Annual averages are calculated using seasonal (quarterly) averages. PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

description: Fishing effort and vessel presence is binned into grid cells 0.01 degrees on a side, and measured in units of hours and published by Global Fishing Watch. The data set's spatial coverage is global and temporal coverage runs from 2012 through 2016. The time is calculated by assigning an amount of time to each AIS detection (which is half the time to the previous plus half the time to the next AIS position), and then summing all positions in each grid cell. Data is based on fishing detections of >70,000 unique AIS devices on fishing vessels. Fishing vessels are identified via a neural network classifier and vessel registry databases. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The Smoke Plume (North America) data set was adapted from the Hazard Mapping System (HMS) Fire and Smoke Analysis product, created by NOAA's Office of Satellite and Product Operations. It displays the detected hot spots and smoke plumes across North America, which may indicate possible fire locations. The data are generated using algorithms for the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES) Imager, the Polar Operational Environmental Satellites (POES), Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR), and Moderate-Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS). Significant smoke plumes are detected by the satellites and are then examined by an analyst for quality control. The analyst outlines the area with an estimate of the smoke concentration provided. This product is created and updated as needed between 1 PM and 11 PM Eastern time. After 11 PM the analysis is fine-tuned as time permits. The graphical HMS product is finalized once daily. The data are available from 2012 to the present. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

The Irrigated Water Requirement and Water Withdrawal data set is prepared by FAO AQUASTAT as part of its Irrigation Water Use study. The data can be used to estimate the amount of irrigation water needed to satisfy crop water demand and compare this with the amount of irrigation water actually used. This provides a measure of a country's shortfall in available irrigation water or irrigation infrastructure. The irrigated water requirement is calculated as irrigation consumptive water use (ICU), which is a function of potential crop evapotranspiration (ETc), effective precipitation (P), and change in soil moisture (DS): ICU = ETc - P - DS Written another way, the irrigation consumptive water use at a point in time (ICU(t)) can be represented as the difference between the potential crop evapotranspiration at time t (ETc(t)) and the actual crop evapotranspiration under nonirrigated conditions at time t (ETa(t)): ICU(t) = ETc(t) - ETa(t) The potential crop evapotranspiration of a grid cell is influenced by certain climatic conditions, such as solar radiation, wind speeds at 2 m, and daily temperatures, among others. The reference evapotranspiration (ETo(t)), determined by the FAO Penman-Monteith equations) in a given area at a given time is the amount of water that would be released into the atmosphere through evapotranspiration if the entire ground surface were covered in a certain crop, typically taken to be grass 12 cm tall, and there were no limits on available water. Each other crop (c) has a crop factor (Kc) that can be used to scale the ETo(t) to obtain ETc(t): ETc(t) = Kc x ETo(t) 118 out of 165 countries in the study report the volume of water used for irrigation to FAO AQUASTAT. For the remaining 47 countries, AQUASTAT developed a method for calculating regional (r) correction ratios (CRr) that relate the total irrigation water requirements for countries in that region (IWRr) to the total irrigation water withdrawn for countries in that region (IWWr). CRr = IWRr / IWWrWhen reliable data on a country's IWW (IWWc) are not available, these values are replaced using the IWRr and CRr of the country's relevant surrounding region: IWWc = IWRr / CRr Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Global Yield Gap Atlas Crop Yield Gap (GYGA-Yg) data compare the performance of crop yields in a location to the theoretically potential yields with no water stress (Yp) and potential yields in presence of some water stress (Yw). Yp and Yw are determined by the biophysical characteristics of the location and the needs of each crop type. This information can be used to identify high- and low-performing crop-growing regions, and to motivate technology and expertise transfer to address suboptimal yields. GYGA-Yg data provide a new perspective in the field of crop yield gap analysis, as they move beyond using gridded climate data to incorporate locally observed climate and production data as much as possible. The smallest unit of analysis for the GYGA-Yg is the region around a reference weather station (RWS). Each RWS is surrounded by a 100-km radius circular buffer. These buffers are then intersected with GYGA climate zones (GYGA-CZs), soil types, and cropping system information. These factors are used as inputs to a crop model to estimate Yw and/or Yp for each RWS buffer zone. GYGA-CZs are defined by growing degree days (GDDs), temperature seasonality, and an annual aridity index (AI), all of which are measured on a 5 arc minute grid. GDDs are defined as the number of days that the mean temperature is above 0°C. Temperature seasonality is calculated to be the standard deviation of the 12 mean monthly temperatures. AI is the ratio of mean annual precipitation over mean annual evapotranspiration. Cropping system information includes the amount of harvested area, the cropping intensity of growth, and aspects of management such as use of irrigation, planting date, and development timeline of various crops. Yield gaps are calculated as the difference between Yw/Yp (simulated yield potential with and without water stress, respectively) and on-farm yields (Ya). Ya are taken from recent national crop-specific yield statistics at the finest resolution available. Ideally, this is at a scale smaller than the GYGA-CZ clipped RWS buffer areas. If national statistics are not available, household surveys that ask about crop production may be used, such as are collected by groups like the World Bank and the Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research (CGIAR). If these are not available, then GYGA country agronomist experts' estimates are used. If there are insufficiently detailed estimates available from country experts, the last resort is to use country-level production statistics.

### Overview The Smoke Plumes (North America) dataset shows the extent and concentration of significant smoke plumes that have been detected across North America in near real-time. The dataset is updated daily with a combination of satellite imagery and algorithms that are verified by satellite analysts. It is presented at a subnational resolution with data from the previous day and the latest seven days. The smoke plumes are categorized by smoke concentration, using the units of low density, medium density, and high density. The dataset was created by the Hazard Mapping System (HMS) Fire and Smoke Analysis product, created by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Office of Satellite and Product Operations (OSPO). It indicates possible locations of fires across North America and should be used for general guidance and strategic planning in response to fires. Additionally, smoke can affect air quality, so understanding the extent of smoke plumes can be a useful tool in assessing air quality throughout North America. ### Methodology The Smoke Plumes dataset is a blended product that used automated fire detection algorithms from the Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellites (GOES) Imager, the Polar Operational Environmental Satellites (POES), Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer (AVHRR), and Moderate-Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS). The algorithms detected significant smoke plumes and the location of possible fires. Satellite analysts examined the data for quality control and outlined the extent of smoke plumes with an estimate of the smoke concentration provided. The product is created every day and updated as needed between 1 PM and 11 PM Eastern time. After 11 PM analysis is fine-tuned as time permits. The graphical HMS product is finalized once daily and archived around 8 AM the following morning. The GOES Imager was used to collect aerosol optical depth using the Aerosol/Smoke Products (GASP) and smoke-specific aerosol optical depth using the GASP Automated Smoke Detection and Tracking Algorithm (ASDTA) at a 2 km resolution . POES AVHRR was used to measure the reflectance of the Earth in five spectral bands at a 1 km resolution. The five spectral bands detected by the instrument were the red (0.6 micrometres), near-infrared (0.9 micrometres), and another three for the thermal radiation emitted by the planet (3.5, 11, and 12 micrometres). MODIS captured data in 36 spectral bands ranging in wavelength from 0.4 micrometers to 14.4 micrometers and at varying spatial resolutions (2 bands at 250 m, 5 bands at 500 m and 29 bands at 1 km). The time spent fishing in each pixel is tracked using a maritime Automatic Identification System (AIS), which is a radio communications system through which vessels continuously broadcast their identity and position using radio signals. Around 300,000 fishing vessels are tracked using this AIS system. From the AIS data, machine-learning classifiers are used to determine the type of ship, its size, what kind of fishing gear it uses, and where and when it is fishing based on its movement patterns. Fishing vessel gear types include six categories: 1) drifting longlines; 2) purse seines (pelagic and demersal); 3) trawlers (all types); 4) fixed_gear (set longlines, set gillnets, and pots and traps); 5) squid jiggers (mostly large industrial pelagic operating vessels); 6) other fishing (a combination of vessels of unknown fishing gear and other, less common gears such as trollers or pole and line). This data set shows the sum of hours spent fishing of each rig type to give the total fishing hours of all rig types. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. We recommend using [this dataset](7b52fb1a-a52d-44b9-bfef-45c3f2610c58) as a replacement.**_ The Ocean Health Index, developed by the National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis (NCEAS) at the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB), measures the global state of the world's oceans. By providing a tool for the ongoing assessment of ocean health, the index can inform policy decisions about how to use or protect marine ecosystems. The Ocean Health Index uses data from global databases to annually assess 221 regions, including all coastal countries, territories, and the Antarctic. The Index is comprised of ten overarching goals that represent the wide range of benefits a healthy ocean can provide: Food Provision, Artisanal Fishing Opportunities, Natural Products, Carbon Storage, Coastal Protection, Tourism & Recreation, Coastal Livelihoods & Economies, Sense of Place, Clean Waters, and Biodiversity. Four dimensions are measured and scored for each goal: status, trend, pressures, and resilience. Present status is a goal’s current value compared to its reference point. Trend is the average percent change of a goal’s status over the most recent five years. Pressures are the ecological and social factors that decrease status. Resilience includes the ecological factors and social initiatives (policies, laws, etc.) that increase status by reducing or eliminating pressures. Scores for the Trend, Pressures and Resilience dimensions are combined as Like Future Status, an indicator of what the status score is likely to be in five years. The Goal Score is the average of the scores for Present Status and Likely Future Status. Status (including Trend) thus makes up 83% of the goal score, while Pressures and Resilience each contribute 8.5%. A region's score, which ranges from 0-100, is the average of its goal scores. The "Earth at Night" map images were generated by National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) using the Suomi National Polar-Orbiting Partnership (Suomi NPP) satellite, managed by NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Suomi NPP observes nearly every location on Earth at roughly 1:30 p.m. and 1:30 a.m. (local time) each day, as it images the planet in vertical 3,000 km (2,000-mile) strips from pole to pole. The satellite’s workhorse instrument is the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), which detects photons of light reflected from the Earth’s surface and atmosphere in 22 different wavelengths. The final Earth at Night products show the areas of man-made visible and infrared light in the world at night, excluding moonlight, fires, and other natural sources of light. Areas with the brightest light points tend to be population centers and are often located in coastal areas. Earth at Night maps are available for the years 2012 and 2016, in both color and grayscale, in both JPEG and GeoTIFF formats and with resolution from 500 m to 3 km. The 2016 images were processed using a compositing technique that selected the best cloud-free nights in each month over each land mass. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. The number of hospitals per county were calculated by determining the location of each hospital, as provided by AHA, and which county each hospital resides, as defined by the TIGER boundary data provided by the US Census Bureau. This dataset provides annual air quality reanalyses for Europe based on both unvalidated (interim) and validated observations. CAMS produces annual air quality (interim) reanalyses for the European domain at significantly higher spatial resolution (0.1 degrees, approx. 10km) than is available from the global reanalyses. The production is currently based on an ensemble of nine air quality data assimilation systems across Europe. A median ensemble is calculated from individual outputs, since ensemble products yield on average better performance than the individual model products. The spread between the nine models can be used to provide an estimate of the analysis uncertainty. The reanalysis combines model data with observations provided by the European Environment Agency (EEA) into a complete and consistent dataset using various data assimilation techniques depending upon the air-quality forecasting system used. Additional sources of observations can complement the in-situ data assimilation, like satellite data. An interim reanalysis is provided each year for the year before based on the unvalidated near-real-time observation data stream that has not undergone full quality control by the data providers yet. Once the fully quality-controlled observations are available from the data provider, typically with an additional delay of about 1 year, a final validated annual reanalysis is provided. Both reanalyses are available at hourly time steps at height levels.

### Overview The Historical Imagery dataset is a compilation of high quality Landsat imagery for each year from 2013-2016. These images show a detailed picture of the landscape at the Earth’s surface, e.g., forests, ice, freshwater, grasslands, desert and urban areas. Landsat data was collected continuously by satellite sensors. These sensors collected approximately 22 complete pictures of the Earth per year, with a spatial resolution of 30 meters (m). The satellite imagery was processed with Google Earth Engine’s Simple Composite algorithm. This algorithm converts the images to [top of atmosphere (TOA) reflectance](https://un-spider.org/node/10958) values and removes cloud-covered pixels. Understanding the Earth’s changing landscape is critical to many environmental issues: agriculture, water usage, forest coverage and natural disasters. In agriculture, Landsat data can be used to predict crop production, help farmers make planting decisions and settle water usage disputes. Landsat imagery shows changes in forest coverage, which is crucial to forest management and protection. Forest coverage influences the environment in many ways, including carbon storage and flood control. Landsat imagery is also a valuable tool for analyzing natural disasters such as floods, fires, droughts and volcanic eruptions. In areas affected by natural disasters, before and after imagery can be used to map damage, plan recovery efforts, and assess future risk. The Historical Imagery dataset was generated by [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/). Earth Engine is a tool for visualizing and analyzing geospatial datasets. The platform hosts satellite imagery in a public data archive for academic, non-profit, business and government users. In addition to hosting data, Earth Engine provides a variety of algorithms and processed datasets, including climate, surface temperature, weather and land cover. Earth Engine is part of Google’s overall mission to organize the world’s information and make it universally accessible. The satellite data used to generate the Historical Imagery dataset was provided by [Landsat](https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/nli/landsat). Landsat is a joint effort between the [United States Geological Survey (USGS)](https://www.usgs.gov/) and the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/). Founded in 1972, Landsat manages satellites that continuously acquire images of the Earth. Landsat’s mission is to provide uninterrupted data and imagery of the Earth to help with decision-making about natural resources and the environment. ### Methodology The Historical Imagery dataset was generated from images of the Earth collected by instruments aboard the [Landsat satellites](https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/nli/landsat/landsat-satellite-missions?qt-science_support_page_related_con=0#qt-science_support_page_related_con). These satellites crossed every point on Earth once every 16 days and each provided 22 complete pictures of the Earth each year. Each pixel in these images has a resolution of 30 m. The satellite imagery was processed using [Google Earth Engine’s Simple Composite algorithm](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/apidocs/ee-algorithms-landsat-simplecomposite). This algorithm selected a subset of pixels at each location and converted them to top of atmosphere (TOA) reflectance. This conversion is a linear transformation used to correct satellite data for variations in solar angle and the scattering of light that occurs as light travels through the atmosphere and reflects off the Earth. The simple cloud score was used to find the images with the least cloud cover. This algorithm scored TOA data pixels by their relative cloudiness from 0 (least cloudy) to 100 (most cloudy). After the pixels were scored, the median of the least cloudy pixels were used, thus selecting the least cloudy images. These images were used to generate the Historical Imagery composites. description: The Certified Commodity Crops Map, created through the research of Chadburn et al. (2017), is the first global data set showing the distribution of commodity crop certification. Crop certification helps consumers purchase more ethical products that come from farms that promote social equality and sustainability. However, these certifications are not well represented in some of the poorest countries of the world or in the tropical rainforests that are at the greatest risk. This map allows users to view the spatial distribution of global crop certification. The locations of certified farms came from publicly available datasets or by directly contacting standards bodies. Certification data from all major standards and codes of practice were included (4C, Bird-friendly coffee, Bonsucro, Etanol Verde, Fairtrade, ISCC, Rainforest Alliance, Roundtable Responsible Soy, Roundtable on Sustainable Biomaterials, Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil, Starbucks C.A.F.E. Practices and UTZ). The seven most certified crops (banana, cocoa, coffee, tea, soybean, sugar and palm oil) were mapped. Coordinates and postal addresses were used to identify point locations of each scheme. Postal addresses were converted to coordinates using ESRI Online World Geocode service. Data cleaning was performed to ensure points were located in their listed country and fell within the crop growing area, identified by a crop cover map. Some data permissions were granted under the condition that they be aggregated with other standards so that specific certification schemes and crop producers could not be identified. Therefore, data were aggregated at a 30 km x 30 km resolution. Certification data came from the years 2013, 2014 and 2015. PREPdata shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

To estimate road traffic fatal injury, countries were classified into 4 groups as follows: (1) Countries with death registration data completeness of at least 80%. For this category, one of the following data points was used: death registration, projection of the most recent death registration, reported death, or projected reported deaths. (2) Countries with other sources of information on cause of death. This group includes India, Iran, Thailand, and Vietnam. For these countries, a regression method was used to project forward the most recent year for which an estimate of total road traffic deaths was available. (3) Countries with population less than 150,000 and without eligible death registration data. For these countries, the deaths reported in the survey were used directly, without adjustment. (4) Countries without eligible death registration data. For these countries, a negative binomial regression model was used. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. The Intact Forest Landscapes (IFL) data set identifies unbroken expanses of natural ecosystems within the zone of forest extent that show no signs of significant human activity and are large enough that all native biodiversity, including viable populations of wide-ranging species, could be maintained. To map IFL areas, a set of criteria was developed and designed to be globally applicable and easily replicable, the latter to allow for repeated assessments over time as well as verification. IFL areas were defined as unfragmented landscapes, at least 50,000 ha in size, and with a minimum width of 10 km. These were then mapped from Landsat satellite imagery for the year 2000. Changes in the extent of IFLs were identified within year 2000 IFL boundary using the global wall-to-wall Landsat image composite for year 2013 and the global forest cover loss data set (Hansen et al. 2013). Areas identified as “reduction in extent” met the IFL criteria in 2000 but no longer met the criteria in 2013. The main causes of change were clearing for agriculture and tree plantations, industrial activity such as logging and mining, fragmentation due to infrastructure and new roads, and fires assumed to be caused by humans. These data can be used to assess forest intactness, alteration, and degradation at global and regional scales. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. RRI recognizes 4 categories of land ownership: (1) owned by indigenous peoples and local communities; (2) designated for indigenous peoples and local communities; (3) administered by governments; and (4) owned by individuals and private firms. Global baseline data were collected through a combination of expert consultancies for 48 countries and in-house desk research on 23 countries. Then the preliminary country data were submitted to people with relevant expertise to verify that the data were as complete as possible and based on the most up-to-date laws and regulations. ### Overview This GIS layer represents the polygon layer for Strategic Water Source Areas (SWSAs) of South Africa, Lesotho and Swaziland. Strategic Water Source Areas are areas that supply a disproportionate amount of mean annual runoff to a geographical region of interest. National Strategic Water Source Areas were derived by grouping mean annual runoff in MAR_SWSA (also in BGIS) into categories representing 10, 30, 50, 75, 90 and 100% of South Africa’s water supply. Those areas supplying ≥ 50% (which were represented by grid cells with ≥ 135 mm/year) were taken to represent national Strategic Water Source Areas and converted to this polygon coverage. The mean annual runoff category, depicting grid cells that contribute > 50, 30 or 10% of the mean annual runoff are provided as attributes, as well as the name of the Strategic Water Source Area. ### Methodology This map is a polygon version created by extracting all grid cells in MAR_SWSA (also on BGIS) with ≥ 135 mm/year and converting them to polygons. The original MAR_SWSA was created using the Water Resources of South Africa data (WR2005) for Mean Annual Runoff at a quaternary catchment scale (Middleton and Bailey 2009), which was then disaggregated to a 1 x 1 minute grid resolution using a set of generalised rainfall-runoff relationships provided by Pitman (1996) and used in the WR90 project (Midgley et al. 1994). The polygons here of Strategic Water Source Areas was produced by grouping areas generating mean annual runoff across South Africa, Lesotho and Swaziland into percentile categories, where areas representing 50% of the mean annual runoff in the region were considered to be Strategic Water Source Areas for the country. The polygons of these areas is given in this data layer. These areas in South Africa, Lesotho and Swaziland together contribute 50% of the region’s water supply in less than 8% of the land surface area. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview The Roadless Areas dataset includes areas that were at least 1 km from roads in 2013.The data also includes an assessment of the roadless areas' status, quality, and extent of coverage by protected areas. Roads fragment landscapes and enable both human colonization and degradation of ecosystems, which harm biodiversity and ecosystem functions. The planet’s remaining large and ecologically important tracts of roadless areas sustain biodiversity and provide ecosystem services on a worldwide scale. Although 80% of Earth’s terrestrial surface remains roadless, this area is fragmented into ~600,000 patches, more than half of which are less than 1 km² and only 7% of which are larger than 100 km². Global protection of ecologically valuable roadless areas is inadequate, and international protection of roadless areas is urgently needed to halt their continued loss. This dataset was created by CEEM/HNEE/OSM and Ibisch et al. (2016) using 2013 OpenStreetMap roads data. ### Methodology This data was collected through two sources: OpenStreetMap and the Global Roads Open Access Data Set (gRoads). OpenStreetmap is a project that maps and updates free global geographic data (focusing on roads) with an open-access, grassroots approach. To determine roadless areas, the authors created a 1 km buffer to all roads. gRoads is an open access global set of roads between settlements using a consistent data model (UNSDI-T v.2). A set of ecological properties that reflect the importance to biodiversity, ecological functions, and ecosystem resilience were used to assess all roadless areas. All three indicators were normalized to between 0 and 100 to calculate an additive and unitless index of the ecological value of each roadless area identified. ### Overview The Gridded Carbon Footprint dataset shows a gridded estimate of absolute and per capita carbon emissions in the year 2013 for 189 countries. The results were produced by the Gridded Global Model of Carbon Footprints (GGMCF) model at a spatial resolution of 250 meters. GGMCF is based on previously available data for carbon footprint (CF), population, and household spending. The model uses urban vs. rural consumption patterns and purchasing power as the main indicators of per capita footprint. Higher purchasing power generally increases the chance of participating in activities that lead to more carbon emissions. The dataset was created by the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) in collaboration with Shinshu University, Yale, and Lund University. Most cities, towns, and rural areas around the world have no carbon footprint data. This dataset provides the first internationally comparable CF estimates for many regions of the world. The results presented here can help develop strategies to reduce carbon footprint. Additionally, this dataset can be used by national governments to locate small regions with disproportionally high emissions rates. ### Methodology The dataset was created in four distinct steps: 1. National CFs of consumption (CFn) data were taken from the Eora multi-region input-output (MRIO) database for the year 2015. This data included 189 countries and accounted for close to 100% of global CO₂ emission. 2. For the EU, UK, USA, Japan, and China, existing subnational CF models were available from a variety of publications. These models were used to separate national CF of consumption data into subnational/regional data CFr. The size of regions ranged from ZIP codes to provinces. In steps 3 and 4 these subnational regions are treated the same as countries. Regions included the disaggregated subnational regions along with countries that are not disaggregated. 3. Within each region, the CFr was further disaggregated into urban and rural residents utilizing urban vs. rural population data and urban vs. rural expenditure pattern data from the World Bank, Eurostat, and US BEA. This data included 113 countries and accounted for 81% of global CO₂ production for the year 2015. 4. The data was subsequently disaggregated to produce CFs of grid cells using gridded population maps and gridded income data. First, the urban and rural grid cells were identified using the Global Human Settlement Layer Settlement Model Grid (GHS-SMOD). Then the CF for each region was disaggregated across the grid cells based on the combined purchasing power of the population living within each grid cell. Carbon footprints are usually directly related to income and purchasing power. The population in each cell was multiplied by the mean purchasing power at that location to calculate the overall purchasing power per grid cell. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology]( https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/aac72a#erlaac72at1). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data on carbon footprints for the top 500 cities in absolute and per capita values are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Overview The HydroBASINS dataset depicts watershed boundaries and sub-basin delineations at a global scale. A watershed is an area of land that drains all surface and groundwater to a common body of water. The boundaries of watersheds provide important geospatial units for many applications, but at a global scale there is a lack of high-quality sources for watershed mapping and analysis. The HydroBasins dataset is part of the HydroSHEDS database ([Hydrological data and maps based on SHuttle Elevation Derivatives](http://www.hydrosheds.org)) which provides hydrographic data layers that allow for the derivation of watershed boundaries for any given location based on the near-global, high-resolution [Shuttle Radar Topology Mission](https://www2.jpl.nasa.gov/srtm/) digital elevation model. The goal of this product is to provide a seamless global coverage of consistently sized and hierarchically nested sub-basins at different scales (from tens to millions of square kilometers), supported by a coding scheme that allows for analysis of watershed topology such as up- and downstream connectivity. The HydroSHEDS database generates key data layers to support regional and global watershed analyses, hydrological modeling, and freshwater conservation planning at a quality, resolution and extent that has previously been unachievable. Watersheds in this database are delineated at 15 arc-second resolution with a hierarchical sub-basin breakdown. The HydroBASINS product was created in 2013. It was developed on behalf of the World Wildlife Fund US (WWF), with support from and in collaboration with the [EU BioFresh] (http://www.freshwaterbiodiversity.eu/contact/) project, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), and McGill University. ### Methodology All HydroBASINS layers were derived from World Wildlife Fund’s [HydroSHEDS data](http://www.hydrosheds.org) based on a grid resolution of 15 arc-seconds (approximately 500 m x 500 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.). An important characteristic of any sub-basin delineation is the sub-basin breakdown, i.e. the decision of when and how to subdivide a larger basin into multiple tributary basins. Standard GIS tools offer the possibility to break out sub-watersheds at any confluence where the inflowing branches (i.e., a tributary and its main stem) exceed a certain size threshold, typically measured by the number of upstream pixels or the upstream catchment area. HydroBASINS divides a basin into two sub-basins at every location where two river branches meet which each have an individual upstream area of at least 100 km². A second critical feature of sub-basin delineations is the way the sub-basins are grouped or coded to allow for the breakout of nested sub-basins at different scales, or to navigate within the sub-basin network from up- to downstream. One of the easiest methods for navigation is to provide the ID of the next downstream object, which allows for moving from object to object in order to traverse the network. As for nesting and topological concepts, the ‘Pfafstetter’ coding system is frequently used due to its relative simplicity and ease of application. The basic principle of the Pfafstetter coding is that a larger basin is sequentially subdivided into 9 smaller units (the 4 largest tributaries, coded with even numbers, and the 5 inter-basins, coded with odd numbers). Thus, the next finer resolution of a sub-basin delineation is achieved at the next Pfafstetter level by adding one digit to the code of the previous level. A more detailed description of the Pfafstetter coding is provided in literature (e.g., [Verdin and Verdin 1999](https://www.bowdoin.edu/~ltoma/teaching/cs3225-GIS/fall16/Project-watershed/papers-watershed/1999-delineate-verdin.pdf)). The HydroBASINS product provides levels 1 to 12 globally. Level 1 distinguishes 9 continents. Level 2 splits each continent into up to 9 large sub-units. Level 3 corresponds to the largest river basins for each continent. From Level 4 onwards, the breakdown follows the Pfafstetter concept. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.hydrosheds.org/images/inpages/HydroBASINS_TechDoc_v1c.pdf) ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Delineations for all Pfafstetter levels (1-12) by region can be downloaded from the the source. A version of this dataset with inserted lakes as well as data for void-filled elevation, hydrologically conditioned elevation, drainage directions, flow accumulation, river networks, basin outlines, lake shorelines, and other hydro-environmental variables is also available from the data provider. The Coral Reef Watch (CRW) program of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAH) produces this daily 5 km product of coral reef bleaching alert areas, allowing direct monitoring of 95% of global coral reefs. This 7-day composite product shows the maximum stress level that an ocean pixel has experienced due to high sea surface temperature (SST) during the most recent 7 consecutive days, and are dated on the last day of the period. These data are used as the core of NOAA's CRW coral bleaching management program. These coral bleaching alerts are derived from the NOAA National Environmental Satellite Data and Information Service (NESDIS) 5 km Geo-Polar Blended Night-Only SST Analysis. Long-term satellite data of SST is used to define the "usual" SST for a given grid cell. This is taken to be the maximum monthly mean SST over that grid cell. For example, if September is the month with the hottest average SST, the September mean SST will be taken as that grid cell's "usual" value. A HotSpot is then defined as temperatures that are higher than this average. A Degree Heating Week is defined as a grid cell being week degree C hotter than usual for a period of one week. The Bleaching Alert Levels are defined as below. This product shows the maximum bleaching alert level that a grid square has reached in the past 7 consecutive days. Stress Level Definition Effect No Stress HotSpot <= 0 Bleaching Watch 0 < HotSpot < 1 Bleaching Warning 1 <= HotSpot and 0 < DHW < 4 Possible Bleaching Bleaching Alert Level 1 1 <= HotSpot and 4 <= DHW < 8 Bleaching Likely Bleaching Alert Level 2 1 <= HotSpot and 8 <= DHW Mortality Likely Full technical details on the types of satellites used, data collected, and analyses performed are available at the following sites: http://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/6/11/11579 and https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/methodology/methodology.php#sst. _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](574f0b71-8363-4e3a-978f-2b1ce58c1c33) as a replacement.**_ ### Overview The Coral Reef Bleaching Alerts dataset shows the maximum amount of coral bleaching stress that an area has experienced over the past seven day period. The dataset is based on bleaching stress caused by high sea surface temperatures (SST). Bleaching stress is determined by comparing historical SST data to near-real-time SST data to view ocean areas that have potentially harmful heat stress levels, especially with regard to accumulated heat stress impacts. For this dataset SST information is used to classify ocean areas into five bleaching alert categories: no stress, bleaching watch, bleaching warning (bleaching is possible), bleaching alert level 1 (bleaching is likely to occur), and bleaching alert level 2 (coral death is likely to occur). The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 5 kilometers (km) and is available for all of earth’s oceans. It is updated daily and displays the highest bleaching alert category the ocean pixel has experience within the last seven days. Coral reefs provide economic goods and services worth about $375 billion each year and are home to over 25% of all marine life. Coral bleaching occurs when a coral expels its symbiotic dinoflagellates (zooxanthellae) due to various environmental stresses. After zooxanthellae are expelled only a white skeleton remains; this phenomenon is known as bleaching. Increased SST of as little as 1 to 2 degrees celsius above normal has been shown to cause bleaching. Extensive bleaching events have dramatic long-term ecological and social impacts, including loss of reef-building corals, changes in benthic habitat, changes in associated fish populations, and economic loss. After a bleaching event it can take decades for severely bleached reefs to fully recover. As the climate continues to warm, bleaching is a major threat to the future of coral reefs. The dataset was created by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) National Environmental Satellite, Data and Information Service (NESDIS) as part of their Coral Reef Watch program. The dataset has proven highly successful in nowcasting mass coral bleaching episodes. It provides reliable global monitoring and prediction of environmental conditions leading to bleaching and is used to guide targeted observations and management responses around the world. ### Methodology The Coral Reef Bleaching Alerts dataset shown on Resource Watch utilizes the NOAA Coral Reef Watch (CRW) daily global 5 km satellite Bleaching Alert Area (7-day maximum) product. It was created by comparing near-real-time sea surface temperature (SST) values with a long-term baseline SST (climatology). The climatology was produced using night-only values for the period 1985–2012 from the 4-km AVHRR Pathfinder Version 5.2 SST (PFV5.2), an official NOAA climate data record. For each pixel (4 km), daily SST data were averaged for each month to produce monthly composites. These were then averaged across the 28-year period to produce 12 monthly mean climatologies. Near-real-time SST values were taken from NOAA National Environmental Satellite Data and Information Service (NESDIS) near-real-time operational daily global 5-km Geo-Polar Blended Night-Only SST Analysis. This NESDIS data is derived from SST measurements taken by a combination of six satellites (four geostationary and two polar-orbiting satellites) operated by NOAA, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) and the European Organisation for the Exploitation of Meteorological Satellites (EUMETSAT). The satellites take as many as 50 SST observations each night over the same location. The final daily SST value for each pixel is a combination of all SST measurements taken each night. Daily SST values were compared to monthly mean climatology to determine anomalies (differences) in daily SSTs. From this information two measurements were created: Coral Bleaching HotSpots and Degree Heating Weeks (DHW). Coral Bleaching HotSpots is a measurement of the magnitude of daily thermal stress that can lead to coral bleaching. It describes the amount of degrees that a daily SST value is higher than the maximum of the monthly mean (MMM) climatology for a pixel. The MMM climatology for any given pixel is the maximum value among the 12-monthly mean SST climatologies for that grid cell. DHW shows the accumulated thermal stress over a prolonged period and has been shown to be predictive of mass coral bleaching. It is an accumulation of all daily HotSpot values that are at least 1°C, over a 12-week period. The final Bleaching Alert Area (BAA) (7-day maximum) dataset is derived from a combination of DHW and HotSpot data. BAA is updated daily, but shows the maximum Alert Level of the preceding seven days. BAA levels are assigned using the following criteria: - No Stress: HotSpot <=0 - Bleaching Watch: 0<HotSpot<1 - Bleaching Warning (possible bleaching): 1<= HotSpot and 0<DHW<4 - Bleaching Alert Level 1 (bleaching likely): 1<=HotSpot and 4<=DHW<8 - Bleaching Alert Level 2 (mortality likely): 1<=HotSpot and 8<=DHW For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for sea surface temperature, sea surface temperature anomaly, coral bleaching hotspots, degree heating week, bleaching alert area (single-day), and sea surface temperature trend (7-day) are available from the data provider. Both a near-real-time and an offline version of each of these datasets are available. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/bio_005_coral_bleaching). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: The Tree Plantations data set was created by Transparent World, with the support of Global Forest Watch. Many studies depicting forest cover and forest change cannot distinguish between natural forests and plantations. This data set attempts to distinguish tree plantations from natural forest for 7 key countries: Brazil, Cambodia, Colombia, Indonesia, Liberia, Malaysia, and Peru. Given the variability of plantations and their spectral similarity to natural forests, this study used visual interpretations of satellite imagery, primarily Landsat, supplemented by high resolution imagery (Google Maps, Bing Maps, or Digital Globe), where available, to locate plantations. Analysts hand-digitized plantation boundaries based on several key visual criteria, including texture, shape, color, and size. Each polygon is labeled with the plantation type and when possible, the species. A “gr” in front of the species name indicates a group of species, such as pines or fruit, where the individual species was not identifiable. The percentage of plantation coverage indicates a rough estimate of the prevalence of plantation within a polygon (as in the case of a mosaic). Types are defined as follows: (1) large industrial plantation: single plantation units larger than 100 ha; (2) mosaic of medium-sized plantations: mosaic of plantation units < 100 ha embedded within patches of other land use; (3) mosaic of small-sized plantations: mosaic of plantation units < 10 ha embedded within patches of other land use; (4) clearing/very young plantation: bare ground with contextual clues suggesting it will become a plantation (shape or pattern of clearing, proximity to other plantations, distinctive road network, etc.). The Urban Heat Island (UHI) effect represents the relatively higher temperatures found in urban areas compared to surrounding rural areas owing to higher proportions of impervious surfaces and the release of waste heat from vehicles and heating and cooling systems. Paved surfaces and built structures tend to absorb shortwave radiation from the sun and release long-wave radiation after a lag of a few hours. The Global Urban Heat Island Data Set, 2013, estimates the land surface temperature in urban areas in degrees Celsius (average summer daytime maximum and average summer nighttime minimum) as well as the difference between those temperatures and the temperatures in surrounding rural areas, defined as a 10 km buffer around the urban extent. Urban extents are from SEDAC’s Global Rural-Urban Mapping Project, Version 1 (GRUMPv1), and land surface temperatures are from SEDAC’s Global Summer Land Surface Temperature (LST) Grids, 2013, which are derived from the Aqua Level-3 Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS), Version 5, global daytime and nighttime Land Surface Temperature (LST) 8-day composite data (MYD11A2). For most regions, the UHI data set provides the average daytime maximum (1:30 p.m. overpass) and average nighttime minimum (1:30 a.m. overpass) temperatures in urban and rural areas, and the urban-rural temperature differences, derived from LST data representing a 40-day time span during July-August (Julian days 185-224) in the Northern Hemisphere and January-February (Julian days 001-040) in the Southern Hemisphere. description: The Global Gridded Model of Carbon Footprints (GGMCF), created by the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), shows a gridded estimate of carbon emissions across 189 countries for the year of 2013 with a 250 square meter resolution. The GGMCF was built in four steps: (1) National Carbon Footprints (CFs) of consumption (*CFn*) for 189 countries covering ~100% of global carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions were taken from the Eora multi-region input-output (MRIO) database for the year 2015. (2) For the EU, UK, USA, Japan, and China, existing subnational CF models were used to disaggregate *CFn* into subnational regions *CFr*, where the regions *r* range in size from postcode to province. In steps 3 and 4 these subnational regions are treated the same as countries. The term 'regions' is used to mean the collection of disaggregated subnational regions plus countries which are not disaggregated. (3) Within each region the *CFr* was disaggregated between urban vs rural residents according to the difference in urban vs rural resident expenditure patterns and the total urban vs rural population. For 76 countries (a mixture of developed and developing coutnries, driving 19% of global CO2 emissions) no comparative expenditure data were available. In these countries all households were assumed to have a national average expenditure pattern. (4) CFs of grid cells within a region were calculated by further disaggregating step 3 using gridded population maps and gridded income data. The first step involved in identifying the urban and rural grid cells and subsequently distributing the total urban and rural footprint on the basis of the share of aggregate purchasing power in each cell. Urban cells were identified using the GHS-SMOD layer of urban areas (high and low density population clusters). GHS-SMOD uses a clustering algorithm to identify urban areas as clusters of contiguous cells within a total population and population density above the specified thresholds. Aggregate purchasing power per grid cell was determined by multiplying the population in the cell by the mean purchasing power at that location. Carbon footprints of cities are then defined as the CF of those cells in teh GHS-SMOD layer that are high-density clusters of contiguous grid cells with ≥1500 inhabitants/km2 and within a minimum population of 50,000. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: LAI was defined by CEOS as half the developed area of the convex hull wrapping the green canopy elements per unit horizontal ground. This definition allows accounting for elements which are not flat such as needles or stems. LAI is strongly non linearly related to reflectance. Therefore, its estimation from remote sensing observations will be scale dependant over heterogeneous landscapes. When observing a canopy made of different layers of vegetation, it is therefore mandatory to consider all the green layers. This is particularly important for forest canopies where the understory may represent a very significant contribution to the total canopy LAI. The derived LAI corresponds therefore to the total green LAI, including the contribution of the green elements of the understory. The product at 333m resolution is provided in Near Real Time and consolidated in the next six periods.

It is closely related to FAPAR and is little scale dependant. Every 10-days estimates are available at global scale in the spatial resolution of about 300m from 2014 to June 2020.

### Overview The Coral Reef Fisheries Relative Catch dataset shows a basic estimate of the relative size of coral reef fisheries catch. This catch is determined as a function of estimated reef productivity and fishing effort. This global data set reflects the world's coral reefs as a 500 meter (m) grid, classified by a relative estimate of the annual fish harvest as of 2014. Reef areas are classified by decile of estimated fisheries catch by weight (biomass). The estimates do not account for variability in the economic or social value of these fisheries. Coral reef fisheries are an important source of food for local populations. They also generate revenue and exports. Furthermore, while most fishing on reefs is artisanal, some coral reefs host a proportion of very high-value target species which attract distant-water fleets. The relative productivity and composition of different reef fisheries is thus both socially and economically significant, and a relevant input to marine management. These estimates represent an important aspect of coral reef value—the relative size and spatial distribution of catch coming from coral reef fisheries—and represent an important incentive for sustainable reef management. The dataset was created by researchers from The Nature Conservancy (TNC), the University of Cambridge (Cambridge), and the World Resources Institute (WRI). ### Methodology Catch is determined as a function of estimated reef productivity and fishing effort. A minor modifier to this basic model makes allowance for no-take fishing areas: within these zones, fishing is not allowed and catches are presumed to be zero; in adjacent waters, a small buffer of enhanced fishery productivity reflects anticipated spillover from these protected areas. The authors do not account for variability in the economic or social value of these fisheries. The estimation of coral-reef associated fisheries involves 4 steps: 1. Estimate the pristine potential maximum sustainable yield (MSY) of coral reefs—the potential sustainable production of fish on healthy reefs. This estimate was based on a review of numerous published estimates of fisheries yields or maximum sustainable yield per unit area world-wide. 2. Estimate the realistic potential MSY on coral reefs, in light of current reef condition (degradation), which can reduce productivity. A proportional reduction was made based on the [Reefs at Risk](https://www.wri.org/publication/reefs-risk-revisited) model of integrated local threat to reefs, along with other studies. 3. Estimate catch based on the potential MSY, adjusted by nearby population and available fishing area, using a model adapted from previous field-based studies: reefs are recorded as reaching maximum fishing effort at population levels greater than 600 persons within reach of each square kilometre of reef. 4. This catch layer was modified for strictly protected no-take zones. Catch values were reduced to zero (no catch) in the no-take zones, while the potential catch in a surrounding 1 km buffer was raised to the maximum value, reflecting anticipated spillover. For more information, please see the source [methodology](https://www.nature.org/content/dam/tnc/nature/en/documents/Atlas-of-Ocean-Wealth.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset.
