This data details projections of poverty rates worldwide and aims at assessing absolute poverty changes at the global level under different scenarios. The model combines country-specific historical estimates of the distribution of income, using Beta–Lorenz curves, with projections of population changes by age and education attainment level, as well as GDP projections to provide the first set of internally consistent poverty projections for all countries of the world. Extreme poverty is defined as living on less than $1.90 a day, measured in 2011 Purchasing Power Parity prices. Making use of demographic and economic projections developed in the context of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), poverty paths are projected by country up to the year 2030. The differences implied by different global scenarios span worldwide poverty rates ranging from 4.5% (around 375 million persons) to almost 6% (over 500 million persons) by the end of our projection period. The largest differences in poverty headcount and poverty rates across scenarios appear for Sub-Saharan Africa, where the projections for the most optimistic scenario imply over 300 million individuals living in extreme poverty in 2030. The results of the comparison of poverty scenarios point towards the difficulty of fulfilling the first goal of the SDGs unless further development policy efforts are enacted. In addition to the baseline scenario, poverty projections based on the other four scenarios which compose the SSPs and which present different narratives about future global socioeconomic developments were computed. These scenarios differ in the importance of challenges to mitigation and challenges to adaptation (i.e., vulnerability) to climate change. SSP1 is characterized by low challenges for both climate change adaptation and mitigation resulting from income growth which does not rely heavily on natural resources and technological change, coupled with low fertility rate and high educational attainment. SSP2 corresponds to the benchmark scenario and assumes the continuation of current global socioeconomic trends at the global level. In SSP3, low economic growth coupled with low educational attainment levels and high population growth at the global level are the main elements of the narrative, which is characterized by high mitigation and adaptation challenges. SSP4 presents a narrative of worldwide polarization, with high income countries exhibiting relatively high growth rates of income, while developing economies present low levels of education, high fertility and economic stagnation. Finally, SSP5 presents a scenario with high economic growth (and therefore low adaptation challenges) coupled with high demand for fossil energy from developing economies, thus increasing global CO2 emissions. ### Overview Accessibility to cities quantifies the time it takes to travel to the nearest urban center via surface transport as of 2015. The dataset uses data on roads, railways, rivers, water bodies, and foot travel on different land cover types. It also includes information on topographical conditions (slope angle and elevation) and additional time for crossing national borders. The dataset was sourced from a variety of resources that each specialize in a specific mode of land transportation. The data was created with the goal of understanding how travel time varies for different urban centers. Urban centers typically have higher concentrations of important resources and infrastructure than rural regions. Improving accessibility to these resources is integral to improving equality around the world. The dataset was created by the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) with travel time in minutes at a 30 arc second spatial resolution (approximately 1 km at the equator). ### Methodology Researchers first created a model that calculated the travel time for each pixel (1 km²) on earth. It was based on travel time information on roads, railways, and bodies of water. Additionally, information on land cover types, topographic conditions (slope and elevation), and national borders were included, as they usually affect travel time. An algorithm was then applied to the model to determine the fastest travel times between destinationsThe road and railway datasets were created by merging Open Street Map (OSM) data with a distance-to-roads product derived from the Google roads database from November 2016 and March 2016. Data on river travel was taken from CIA World Data Bank II vector rivers dataset, lake travel from global surface-water occurrence dataset, and ocean travel from the automatic Identification System (AIS) and Voluntary Observing Ship (VOS) program. Undeveloped land was given a baseline speed of movement (by foot) using the MODIS MCD12Q1 land cover product. The final data was adjusted to account for topographical properties using Global Multi-resolution Terrain Elevation Dataset 2010 (GMTED2010) and a one hour travel penalty was added for any border crossing. An urban center is defined as a contiguous area with 1,500 or more inhabitants per km² or a majority of built-up land cover coincident with a population center of at least 50,000 inhabitants. Cities were identified using the above assumption based on the Global Human Settlement Grid of High-Density Land Cover (GHS-HDC) data set and country borders were taken from the UN Global Administrative Units Layer (GAUL). Because cities are typically clusters of many cells rather than individual points, they are effectively treated as polygons when calculating travel time from a given point. The accessibility surface map was generated using the cumulative cost function within Google Earth Engine. The map was validated by testing its travel time calculations between 53,091 points compared to travel time estimates calculated by Google Maps. The final accessibility map was presented in raster format with a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds (around 1 km at the equator). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature25181). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. As part of the World Climate Research Program Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6), the international community is developing the next generation of advanced Earth System Models (ESM) able to estimate the combined effects of human activities (e.g. land use and fossil fuel emissions) on the carbon-climate system. In addition, a set of historical data based on HYDE, and multiple alternative scenarios of the future (2015-2100) developed by Integrated Assessment Model (IAM) teams, are being developed as input for these models. The goal of the Land-Use Harmonization (LUH2) project is to prepare a harmonized set of land-use scenarios that smoothly connects the historical reconstructions of land-use with the future projections in the format required for ESMs. The land-use harmonization strategy estimates the global fractional land-use patterns, underlying land-use transitions, and key agricultural management information, annually for the time period 850-2100 at 0.25° x 0.25° resolution, while minimizing the differences at the transition between the historical reconstruction ending conditions and IAM initial conditions, and working to preserve changes depicted by the IAMs in the future. Please see publications for more detail on the development of the Land-Use Harmonization model. In this data set Resource Watch displays the land-use patterns of the projected section of data (2015 – 2100) under RCP 2.6 SSP1 (from IMAGE), and classified pixels as the land use category that had the maximum fractional cover. RCP2.6 (also referred to as RCP3PD) represented a very low emission scenario and explores the feasibility of limiting climate change to less than 2°C by limiting radiative forcing to a peak of 3 Wm^−2 in mid-century, declining to 2.6 W/m^2 in 2100.

### Overview Relative change in crop yield shows climate projections for crop yield at the national and sub-national levels under different concentration pathways (RCP 4.5 and 8.5). Data is aggregated annually for either national or sub-national boundaries and depict changes in crop yield over time from 2015 through 2050. Changes in yield are compared to the reference period of 1986-2006 and are shown in percentages. Understanding how climate change will affect crop yields is important for agricultural planning, food security, and global commodity flows. This dataset provides needed information on how climate change will impact yield under several emissions scenarios at the country and provincial levels and for near- and longer-term timeframes. The global economy is intimately tied to agricultural production, and this provides insight into future changes that will have impact on global systems. Climate Analytics is dedicated to advancing scientific literacy of climate change and providing support and capacity building to stakeholders. They support science-based policy to enable sustainable development and provide solutions to climate change policy challenges. ### Methodology Input data for crop yield change uses greenhouse gas concentration scenarios derived from the Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) framework, which was developed within the Coupled Intercomparison Modeling Project 5 (CMIP5) and is widely used in the climate modeling community. RCP 4.5 depicts an intermediate scenario whereas 8.5 represents a high emissions pathway. Other data is derived from the Inter-Sectoral Impact Model Intercomparison Project (ISIMIP), which provides changes in biophysical systems and extreme events. Climate projections for crop yield were modeled for different emissions scenarios from 2015 to 2100 and are compared against the baseline period of 1986-2006. Results show the annual average changes in crop yield over the area of interest (national/sub-national levels). Projections of future impacts to changes in crop yield are calculated assuming that socio-economic (population, land-use, etc.) factors remain constant at 2005 levels. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://climate-impact-explorer.climateanalytics.org/methodology/). ### Additional Information Our data catalog also shows Relative Humidity data from Climate Analytics. Additional projections for other crops, impacts, emissions scenarios, and timeframes are also produced by Climate Analytics. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/foo_069_rw0_relative_change_crop_yield). This data has been mapped on our data catalog by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](cf069d6d-27b0-4282-8ff3-ee04d90e841d) as a replacement.**_ The Gender Development Index (GDI), published by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), measures gender gaps in human development achievements by accounting for disparities between women and men in 3 basic dimensions of human development using the same component indicators as in the Human Development Index (HDI). The HDI is a summary measure of average achievement in key dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, being knowledgeable, and a decent standard of living. The HDI is the geometric mean of normalized indices for each of the 3 dimensions. The health dimension is assessed by life expectancy at birth; the education dimension is measured by mean of years of schooling for adults aged 25 years and more and expected years of schooling for children of school-entering age. The standard-of-living dimension is measured by gross national income per capita. The HDI uses the logarithm of income to reflect the diminishing importance of income with increasing gross national income (GNI). The scores for the 3 HDI dimension indices are then aggregated into a composite index using geometric mean. The GDI is the ratio of the HDIs calculated separately for females and males using the same methodology as in the HDI. It is a direct measure of gender gap, showing the female HDI as a percentage of the male HDI. The GDI is calculated for 161 countries in 2015 and shows how much women are lagging behind their male counterparts in each dimension of human development. It facilitates understanding of the real gender gap in human development achievements and is useful in designing policy tools to close the gap. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The Dynamic World (Land Cover product) dataset shows globally consistent, high resolution, near real-time (NRT) land use land cover (LULC) classification leveraging deep learning on 10 meters Sentinel-2 imagery. The dataset was created utilizing a highly scalable cloud-based system to apply this approach and provide an open, continuous feed of LULC predictions in parallel with Sentinel-2 acquisitions. The dataset includes the following Land Cover types: water, trees, grass, flooded vegetation, crops, shrub/scrub, built area, bare ground, and snow/ice. You can learn more about the dataset [here](http://dynamicworld.app). Regularly updated global land use land cover (LULC) datasets provide the basis for understanding the status, trends, and pressures of human activity on carbon cycles, biodiversity, and other natural and anthropogenic processes. Annual maps of global LULC have been developed by many groups and while widely used, many important LULC change processes are difficult or impossible to observe at a spatial resolution greater than 100 meters and annual temporal resolution, such as emerging settlements and small-scale agriculture and early stages of deforestation and wetland/grassland conversion. Inability to resolve these processes introduces significant errors in our understanding of ecological dynamics and carbon budgets. Thus, there is a critical need for spatially explicit, moderate resolution (10-30 meters/pixel) LULC products that are updated with greater temporal frequency. The Dynamic World dataset is a first-of-its-kind NRT product, which accommodates a variety of user needs ranging from extremely up-to-date LULC data to custom global composites representing user-specified date ranges. Furthermore, the continuous nature of the product's outputs enables refinement, extension, and even redefinition of the LULC classification. In combination, these attributes enable unprecedented flexibility for a diverse community of users across a variety of disciplines. ### Methodology The classification schema for Dynamic World was determined after a review of global LULC maps. The Dynamic World taxonomy maintains a close semblance to the land use classes presented in the [IPCC Good Practice Guidance](https://www.ipcc-nggip.iges.or.jp/public/gpglulucf/gpglulucf.html) to ensure easier application of the resulting data for estimating carbon stocks and greenhouse gas emissions. The modeling approach relies on semi-supervised deep learning and requires spatially dense annotations. To collect a diverse set of training and evaluation data, the authors divided the world into three regions, then further divided each region by the [14 RESOLVE Ecoregions biomes](https://academic.oup.com/bioscience/article/67/6/534/3102935). At each sample location, an initial selection of Sentinel-2 images from 2019 scenes based on image cloudiness metadata reported in the Sentinel-2 tile’s QA60 band was selected. The authors further filtered scenes to remove images with many masked pixels. Individual tiles of 510x510 pixels centered on the sample sites from random dates in 2019 were finally extracted. Further steps were then taken to obtain an “as balanced as possible” training dataset with respect to the LULC classifications from the respective LULC products. To achieve a large dataset of labeled Sentinel-2 scenes, the authors worked with two groups of annotators: photo-interpretation experts (validating 4,000 tiles) and non-experts (validating 20,000 tiles). A final validation set of 409 image tiles were held back from the modeling effort and used for evaluation as described in the Technical Validation section of the source methodology. To account for an annotation skill differential between the non-expert and expert groups, they one-hot encode the labeled pixels and smooth them according to the confidence in a binary label of the individual annotator (expert/non-expert). For training data collection, the authors used the Sentinel-2 Level-2A (L2A) product, which provides radiometrically calibrated surface reflectance (SR). However, systematically produced Sentinel-2 SR products are currently only available from 2017 onwards. Therefore, for the modeling approach, the authors used the Level-1C (L1C) product, which was generated from 2015 and represents Top-of-Atmosphere (TOA) reflectance measurements. For any L2A image, there is a corresponding L1C image, allowing them to directly map annotations performed using L2A imagery to the L1C imagery used in model training. In addition to their preliminary cloud filtering in training image selection, the authors adopted and applied a novel masking solution that combines several existing products and techniques, including masking cloud shadows. The distribution of Sentinel-2 reflectance values is highly compressed towards the low end of the sensor range, with the remainder mostly occupied by high return phenomena like snow and ice, bare ground, and specular reflection. To combat this imbalance, the authors introduce a normalization scheme that better utilizes the useful range of Sentinel-2 reflectance values for each band. Their broad approach to transferring the supervised label data to a system that could be applied globally was to train a Fully Convolutional Neural Network (FCNN). Conceptually, this approach transforms pre-processed Sentinel-2 optical bands into a discrete probability distribution of the classes in our taxonomy on the basis of spatial context. This is done per image on the hypothesis that sufficient spatial and spectral context is available to recover one of their taxonomic labels at a pixel. The authors introduce a number of novel innovations that achieve state-of-the-art performance on LULC globally with a neural network architecture almost 100x smaller than architectures used for semantic segmentation or regression of ground-level camera imagery. To generate the NRT products, the authors apply the normalization described earlier to the raw Sentinel-2 L1C imagery and pass all normalized bands except B1, B8A, B9, and B10 after bilinear upscaling to ee.Model.predictImage. This output is then masked using the cloud mask derived from the unnormalized L1C image. The creation of these images is triggered automatically when new Sentinel-2 L1C and S2C images are available.The NRT collection is continuously updated with new results. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: This layer shows the risk of erosion around the world, from low to high. Erosion and sedimentation by water involves the process of detachment, transport, and deposition of soil particles, driven by forces from raindrops and water flowing over the land surface. Because soil erosion is difficult to measure at large scales, soil erosion models are crucial estimation tools to extrapolate limited data to other localities and conditions. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE), which predicts annual soil loss from rainfall and runoff, is the most common model used at large spatial scales due to its relatively simple structure and empirical basis. The model takes into account rainfall erosivity, topography, soil erodibility, land cover and management, and conservation practices. Because the RUSLE model was developed based on agricultural plot scale and parameterized for environmental conditions in the USA, modifications of the methods and data inputs are necessary to make the equation applicable to the globe. We estimated erosion potential based on the RUSLE model, adjusted to extend its applicability to a global scale. Conservation practices and topography information were not included in this model to calculate global erosion potential, due to data limitation and their relatively minor contribution to the variation in soil erosion at the continental to global scale compared to other factors. The result of the global model was categorized into five quantiles, corresponding to low to high erosion risks. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. ### Overview This dataset represents the cost of action to deliver sustainable water management as outlined in the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 6(SDG6). The datasets presented on Resource Watch encompass the water challenges within SDG6 and show the cost percentage each category requires out of the total cost to achieve sustainable water management. Total Estimated Cost is the annual cost in 2015 USD to deliver on each aspect of sustainable water management, calculated for each country as the cost of action required to close the gap between current and desired conditions. This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) to provide a visual representation of the cost to achieve sustainable water management. Water related issues are already a serious concern and will only worsen given the combined effects of population growth, economic growth, and climate change. SDG6 works to “ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all” by 2030. Sustainable water management includes access to drinking water, access to sanitation services, water pollution, water scarcity, and water management. Each of these categories has specific "estimated cost" and its percentage of the "total estimated cost" can communicate the relative magnitude of the issue, from a financial perspective. This cost does not fully account for the social and economic benefits of resolving each water challenge and should not be used to inform local policy decisions. ### Methodology This dataset calculates the cost of action to close the gap between current and desired sustainable water management conditions by 2030. Where possible, the calculation method builds off of existing research and methods rather than developing new approaches to calculating the cost of action. The dataset shows values for the total estimated cost to deliver drinking water, deliver access to sanitation services, eliminate industrial water pollution, eliminate agricultural water pollution, address water scarcity, and address water resource management. Each of these categories was created using the formula below: Total Estimated Cost = Projected Gap x Solution Cost The projected gap is the gap between current and desired conditions. The solution cost is the cost, in 2015 US dollars, that it will take to change each unit of the current condition to the desired condition for the population in 2030. Water management is a quantity that is based on population, so to determine the amount of water required for the population in 2030 estimated population data was taken from 2030 gridded population data in Downscaling Drivers of Global Environmental Change: Enabling Use of Global SRES Scenarios at the National and Grid Levels (Hutton and Varughese 2016). Values for the solution cost of creating access to drinking water and sanitation were taken from the World Bank for 140 low-income countries and estimated for all other countries. Solution costs for industrial water pollution were taken from Hutton and Varughese 2016, for agricultural water pollution from a combination of eight academic articles, and for water scarcity from 2030 Water Resources Group (WRG) reports. The proposed method was designed to be reproducible with data at any scale, however this dataset has been developed using global, comparable data. For full discussion of the calculation method, see the Achieving Abundance Technical Appendix. The final datasets were presented as the percentage of costs to achieve each individual form of water management out of the total cost of water management by 2030. The datasets were projected on a global map at a national resolution using vector format. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/resources/data-sets/achieving-abundance). ### Additional Information The percentage of the total estimated cost to address water resources management is 17% for each country, but this indicator was not shown on Resource Watch map. Please click on the “Table” button in the “Customize Visualization” section to find this data on Resource Watch. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](2063964b-56c8-4080-b2a5-5a7710f321b9) as a replacement.**_ Global Solar Atlas' solar irradiation dataset was developed by Solargis and provided by the World Bank Group. Solar resource, PV power potential, and air temperature data is aggregated long-term into yearly averages. The PV energy simulation is based on the use of re-computed and statistically aggregated 15-minute solar resource and air temperature data. This approach is consistent in terms of space and time, and it is provided as a quick assessment tool for exploration, site prospection and pre-feasibility analysis. The global horizontal irradiation (GHI) reflects the sum of direct and diffuse components of solar radiation. GHI is one of the principal climate phenomena that determines solar power generation and is considered a climate reference as it enables comparing individual sites or regions. Photovoltaic electricity output, or power potential, is the amount of energy, converted by a PV system into electricity (kWh/kWp) that is expected to be generated according to the geographical conditions of a site and a configuration of the PV system. Three configurations of a PV system are considered: (i) Small residential; (ii) Medium-size commercial; and (iii) Ground-mounted large scale. The data have a resolution of 1 km and spatial coverage between latitudes 60°N to 45°S. The data represent a time period from January 1994/1999/2007 until December 2015, depending on the satellite coverage. Presently, Solargis processes data from three satellite data providers (EUMETSAT, Japanese Meteorological Agency and National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) with geostationary satellites operating at five key positions, to cover the entire world (except polar and subpolar regions). description: This data set, created by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland and supported by Global Forest Watch, is the first Landsat-based alert system for tree cover loss. While most existing loss alert products use 250 m resolution MODIS imagery, these alerts have a 30 m resolution and thus can detect loss at a much finer spatial scale. The alerts are currently operational for select countries in the Amazon, Congo Basin, and Southeast Asia and will eventually be expanded to the rest of the humid tropics. New Landsat 7 and 8 images are downloaded as they are posted online at USGS EROS, assessed for cloud cover or poor data quality, and compared to the 3 previous years of Landsat-derived metrics (including ranks, means, and regressions of red, infrared, and shortwave bands, and ranks of NDVI, NBR, and NDWI). The metrics and the latest Landsat image are run through 7 decision trees to calculate a median probability of forest disturbance. Pixels with probability > 50% are reported as tree cover loss alerts. For more information on methodology, see the paper in Environmental Research Letters. Alerts remain unconfirmed until 2 or more out of 4 consecutive observations are labeled as tree cover loss. Alerts that remain unconfirmed after subsequent observations are removed from the data set. You can choose to view only confirmed alerts in the menu, but keep in mind that using only confirmed alerts misses the newest detections of tree cover loss. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](dc5db1e0-12bb-4d4d-b84f-37fa492060b6) as a replacement.**_ This layer shows the risk of erosion around the world, from low to high. Erosion and sedimentation by water involves the process of detachment, transport, and deposition of soil particles, driven by forces from raindrops and water flowing over the land surface. Because soil erosion is difficult to measure at large scales, soil erosion models are crucial estimation tools to extrapolate limited data to other localities and conditions. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE), which predicts annual soil loss from rainfall and runoff, is the most common model used at large spatial scales due to its relatively simple structure and empirical basis. The model takes into account rainfall erosivity, topography, soil erodibility, land cover and management, and conservation practices. Because the RUSLE model was developed based on agricultural plot scale and parameterized for environmental conditions in the USA, modifications of the methods and data inputs are necessary to make the equation applicable to the globe. We estimated erosion potential based on the RUSLE model, adjusted to extend its applicability to a global scale. Conservation practices and topography information were not included in this model to calculate global erosion potential, due to data limitation and their relatively minor contribution to the variation in soil erosion at the continental to global scale compared to other factors. The result of the global model was categorized into five quantiles, corresponding to low to high erosion risks. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The NASA-USDA Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) Global Soil Moisture data set is produced by the NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Hydrologic Science Laboratory in collaboration with the USDA Foreign Agricultural Services and the USDA Hydrology and Remote Sensing Lab. This data set provides 3-day composites of global soil moisture estimates from April 1, 2015 to present. This data set includes both surface and subsurface soil moisture estimates (mm), as well as percent soil moisture (%). SMAP Level 3 soil moisture observations are collected with a satellite-based, L-band radar and radiometer instrument. This satellite covers the globe every three days, providing high-resolution data with an accuracy of 0.04 m³/m³. SMAP data are assimilated into the modified Palmer two-layer soil moisture model with a 1-D Ensemble Kalman filter approach. The assimilation of this SMAP data is done to correct model-based soil moisture predictions that can be prone to errors in regions with limited rain gauge data. This data set, created by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland and supported by Global Forest Watch, is the first Landsat-based alert system for tree cover loss. While most existing loss alert products use 250 m resolution MODIS imagery, these alerts have a 30 m resolution and thus can detect loss at a much finer spatial scale. The alerts are currently operational for select countries in the Amazon, Congo Basin, and Southeast Asia and will eventually be expanded to the rest of the humid tropics. New Landsat 7 and 8 images are downloaded as they are posted online at USGS EROS, assessed for cloud cover or poor data quality, and compared to the 3 previous years of Landsat-derived metrics (including ranks, means, and regressions of red, infrared, and shortwave bands, and ranks of NDVI, NBR, and NDWI). The metrics and the latest Landsat image are run through 7 decision trees to calculate a median probability of forest disturbance. Pixels with probability > 50% are reported as tree cover loss alerts. For more information on methodology, see the paper in Environmental Research Letters. Alerts remain unconfirmed until 2 or more out of 4 consecutive observations are labeled as tree cover loss. Alerts that remain unconfirmed after subsequent observations are removed from the data set. You can choose to view only confirmed alerts in the menu, but keep in mind that using only confirmed alerts misses the newest detections of tree cover loss. This data set was obtained directly from the Department of Farmer Welfare and Agriculture Development, Madhya Pradesh and visualized through PREPdata.

description: This global cropping intensity product is the first 30m resolution cropping intensity dataset covering global extent. Based on the reconstructed time series of Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) from multiple satellite images including Landsat-8, Sentinel-2 and MODIS, 30-m planetary-scale pixel by pixel cropping intensity products were generated by enumerating the total number of valid cropping cycles using a binary crop phenophase profile indicating growing and non-growing periods. The total number of valid cropping cycles were also divided by 3 (three years from 2016 to 2018) to retrieve the average cropping intensity. Based on the Google Earth Engine (GEE) cloud computing platform, we implemented our algorithm across the globe to the global cropping intensity products.

The Global Human Modification of Terrestrial Systems data set provides a cumulative measure of the human modification of terrestrial lands across the globe at a 1-km resolution. It is a continuous 0-1 metric that reflects the proportion of a landscape modified, based on modeling the physical extents of 13 anthropogenic stressors and their estimated impacts using spatially-explicit global data sets with a median year of 2016.

### Overview This dataset from the Global Infrastructure Hub (GI Hub) shows national infrastructure investment gaps in 2015 U.S. dollars for the following sectors: energy, telecommunications, airports, ports, rail, road, and water. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total sectors. An investment gap represents the difference between the amount of money a country would need to invest in infrastructure to match the performance of other countries within the same income group and the amount that countries would be likely to spend if trends continued.The investment gap of a country where the investment trends meet their future investment needs is zero. This dataset was developed by the Global Infrastructure Hub. The data covers a total of 56 countries for the years 2016 to 2040. ### Methodology The Global Infrastructure Outlook was calculated using a “top-down” approach, beginning with existing cross-country datasets on infrastructure spending and filling in data gaps, where necessary. Sources for the initial cross-country datasets include the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Infrastructure in Latin America (INFRALATAM), and Eurostat. The infrastructure investment gap for each year was calculated as the difference between the amount of money a country would need to invest in infrastructure to match the performance of other countries within the same income group and the amount that countries would be likely to spend if trends continued for that year. Gaps in national data were filled using data from national statistics agencies and major infrastructure companies. In areas where no data sources could be identified, econometric estimation was used to compute values. In countries where a time series existed but was incomplete, further manipulation was often required to fill in the gaps in that series. For data gaps in the middle of a time series, interpolation was used to fill the gaps. When data was missing from the beginning or the end of the time series, forecasting and/or backcasting were used to develop a longer time series. In the case where data was attributed to a broader sector, secondary data sources were used to align the data with the preferred sector definition. In some countries, data related to investment in utilities was used to attribute the investment into more detailed sectors like water and energy. For example, if energy accounts for 60% of the country's utilities investment, then 60% of the utilities investment would be allocated to the energy sector. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://cdn.gihub.org/outlook/live/methodology/Global+Infrastructure+Outlook+-+July+2017.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. ### Overview This dataset shows solid waste generation, in millions of metric tons per year, at the national level in 2016. Solid waste management is a universal issue that affects daily health, productivity and the cleanliness of communities. Waste management is an expensive and complicated operation, which creates challenges to local administrations. Collecting waste management data is essential to creating policy and plans. With accurate data on waste generation and composition, governments can allocate realistic budgeting and land, and consider relevant technologies and partners for management strategies. The World Bank created this dataset by compiling the best available municipal solid waste management data for 217 countries in 2016. This dataset defines municipal solid waste as residential, commercial, and institutional waste. Industrial, medical, hazardous, electronic, and construction and demolition waste are reported separately from total national waste generation to the extent possible. ### Methodology The World Bank Group compiled solid waste management data from the best available sources and publications. Every effort has been made to verify sources and find the most recent information available. Estimated data is calculated in the case of missing data for 31 countries in the Sub-Saharan Africa region and 8 countries in other regions. This methodology uses the World Bank’s dataset on gross domestic product (GDP) per capita based on purchasing power parity (PPP) in 2011 international dollars in conjunction with United Nations population statistics. It is assumed that waste generation is linked to two factors: - **GDP growth**: As a country advances economically, its per capita waste generation rates increase. Economic growth is reflected using GDP per capita. - **Population growth**: As a country’s population grows, the amount of total waste generated rises. If waste generation data for a country had been reported for 2016, the original data was used. When this data was not available, a regression model was developed to estimate the expected growth in a country’s waste generation rate, based on GDP per capita. The adjusted per capita waste generation rate for 2016 is multiplied by the population in 2016. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/30317). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for country level waste composition, collection, treatment and disposal, and municipal waste management financials are available from the data provider. Because urban data is essential for decision-making and benchmarking, the data provider also reports data from 367 cities. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The traffic deaths rate data produced by the World Health Organization (WHO) give mortality data from road traffic injuries. To estimate road traffic fatal injury, countries were classified into 4 groups as follows: (1) Countries with death registration data completeness of at least 80%. For this category, one of the following data points was used: death registration, projection of the most recent death registration, reported death, or projected reported deaths. (2) Countries with other sources of information on cause of death. This group includes India, Iran, Thailand, and Vietnam. For these countries, a regression method was used to project forward the most recent year for which an estimate of total road traffic deaths was available. (3) Countries with population less than 150,000 and without eligible death registration data. For these countries, the deaths reported in the survey were used directly, without adjustment. (4) Countries without eligible death registration data. For these countries, a negative binomial regression model was used. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. ### Overview Biodiversity hotspots, a classification system created by the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF), include some of our planet’s most biologically diverse yet threatened terrestrial areas. An area is qualified as a hotspot if it contains at least 1,500 species of vascular plants found nowhere else on Earth (known as “endemic” species) and it has lost at least 70 percent of its primary native vegetation. Between 1988 and 2016, 36 biodiversity hotspots have been identified globally. ### Methodology Hotspots were defined by Norman Myers in 1988 when he published a seminal paper identifying 10 tropical forest “hotspots.” These regions were characterized both by exceptional levels of plant endemism, meaning plants found nowhere else on Earth, and serious levels of habitat loss. Conservation International (CI) adopted Myers’s hotspots as its institutional blueprint in 1989. In 1999, CI undertook a global review, which introduced quantitative thresholds for the designation of biodiversity hotspots and resulted in the identification of 25. In 2005, an additional analysis brought the total number of biodiversity hotspots to 34, based on the work of nearly 400 specialists. In 2011, the Forests of East Australia were identified as the 35th hotspot by a team of researchers from the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization working with CI. In February 2016, the North American Coastal Plain was recognized as meeting the criteria and became the world’s 36th hotspot. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Nighttime Imagery (Day/Night Band, Enhanced Near Constant Contrast) is available from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) on the joint NASA/NOAA Suomi National Polar orbiting Partnership (SNPP) satellite. The VIIRS Nighttime Imagery layer shows the earth’s surface and atmosphere using a sensor designed to capture low-light emission sources, under varying illumination conditions. It is displayed as a grey-scale image. Sources of illumination include both natural and anthropogenic sources of light emissions. Lunar reflection can be used to highlight the location and features of clouds and other terrestrial features such as sea ice and snow cover when there is partial to full moon conditions. When there is no moonlight, natural and anthropogenic night time light emissions are highlighted such as city lights, lightning, auroras, fires, gas flares, and fishing fleets. The VIIRS sensor collects imagery as it orbits the Earth every 100 minutes. Passing over the poles 14 times per day, it crosses the equator at at 1:30am local time, photographing the entire world each day. The sensor resolution is 750 m at nadir and the imagery resolution is 500 m. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description: NaturalEarth's Populated Places data set provides geographical locations for cities and towns of regional significance around the world in 2016. Population estimates sourced from LandScan are available for 90% of the contained cities. LandScan uses subnational spatial data sets to disaggregate national census statistics to subnational administrative boundaries. The data and models used to do so are tailored to match the data conditions and geographical nature of each individual country and region. Population values are provided to account for the total metropolitan population, rather than the administrative boundary population. UN metropolitan population estimates are used instead of LandScan for the ~500 largest urban areas in the world. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. This tile layer of the world's hydrological features was created by ESRI and is designed to provide a hydrologically oriented set of features to use with the World Terrain Base Layer or other simple base maps. The map features a hydrocentric design based on the amount of water flowing within the drainage network such that symbols of the same size and color represent roughly the same amount of water. Surface water flow is shown as a linear phenomenon even over and through bodies of water. Using the best available, these data show relative flow accurately, so that if one river carries more water downstream than another river, the result will be that the first river will have a thicker symbol on the map. This map is used as an overlay for content such as elevation from the World Terrain Base service or thematic services such as soil units, vegetation, or ecoregions. Combined with a basemap and map services, this map provides a frame of reference for showing regional, national, and continental hydrologic phenomena such as drought, runoff, river-level monitoring, and flood forecasting. River names are collected in the UTF8 character set so river names are collected in their original language but are written in the Roman alphabet. Sources for all river names are from the open source geonames.org project, so they are international by nature. The map is compiled from several sources. The global scales (very small scales through 1:2,300,000) include content from HydroSHEDS, GTOPO30 Global Topographic Data, SRTM, GLWD, WorldClim, GRDC, and WWF Global 200 Terrestrial Eco Regions, with the latter 3 providing the inputs and basis for calculating flow. At medium scales (1:36,000 to 1:2,000,000) this service currently contains only U.S. data from the NHDPlusV2 that was jointly produced by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). First defined in 1988 by scientist Norman Myers, biodiversity hotspots are areas characterized by high levels of endemic plants coupled with significant habitat loss. Endemism is the ecological state of a species being unique to a defined geographic location, such as an island, nation, country or other defined zone, or habitat type. Specifically, a region must meet the following criteria to achieve the hotspot classification formulated by Conservation International (CI): (1) at least 1,500 species of vascular plants (>0.5% of the world’s total) are endemic; and (2) at least 70% of the original natural vegetation has been lost. When Myers first defined the term, he identified 10 tropical forest hotspots. The need to pinpoint priority conservation regions led CI to adopt the term and reassess the hotspot concept. In this process, CI introduced quantitative thresholds (see above) and added additional regions. At that time, there were 25 hotspots. Because of the constant change in environmental threats and the improved understanding of biodiversity, CI has since revisited the hotspots to refine boundaries, update information, and add new regions to create this global data set. This process produced an additional 10 hotspots, bringing the total to 35. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

### Overview The Total Suspended Matter (TSM) dataset shows the concentration of inorganic particulate matter in seawater in grams per cubic meter (g/m³). The specific data products shown on Resource Watch originate with the [Ocean Land Color Instrument](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/user-guides/sentinel-3-olci) B (OLCI B), a sensor carried by the [Sentinel-3B satellite](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/missions/sentinel-3). An equivalent product for Sentinel-3A is available from the provider. This monthly and 8-day global products have a resolution of 1/24 degrees (°) at the equator (about 4.63 kilometers); between the two satellites, the time series run back to 2016. Like all similar [GlobColour datasets](https://www.globcolour.info/products_description.html), monthly and 8-day "Level-3" TSM is derived from the accumulated data of the daily [Level-2 product](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-3-olci/level-2/ocean-processing) across that month. In the case of TSM, the monthly values represent a simple average of the daily values. TSM is a measure of turbidity: the haziness of a liquid due to suspended particles. Runoff water can carry clay, silt, and other matter from land into the ocean. As the turbidity of water increases, it becomes denser and less clear due to a higher concentration of these light-blocking particles. This in turn can have a wide variety of effects including: reduced sunlight reaching plants and animals, affecting the growth of plankton; increased water temperatures and altered transportation of heat through the water column; and decreased visibility. Ocean color is an "essential climate variable" needed to support the carbon cycle monitoring requirements of the [UNFCCC (United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change)](http://unfccc.int/2860.php). It is also a climate variable that cannot be globally monitored without using satellite observations. In order to cover the long time span necessary for climate monitoring purposes, the required ocean color dataset can only be built by merging together observations made with different satellite systems. The GlobColour project started in 2005 to provide a continuous dataset of merged [Level-3 Ocean Colour](https://www.globcolour.info/CDR_Docs/GlobCOLOUR_PUG.pdf) products. Merging outputs from different sensors ensures data continuity, improves spatial and temporal coverage, and reduces data noise. ### Methodology The monthly, Level-3 TSM product represents an average of the constituent Level-2 inputs, as is the 8-day TSM product. The [ocean processing](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-3-olci/level-2/ocean-processing) component of OLCI Level-2 processing is dedicated to handling water pixels. It is divided into two main tasks: atmospheric correction and ocean color processing. Atmospheric correction follows two approaches; the "standard" or "baseline" approach, further split into atmosphere characterisation and correction, and an "alternative" approach in which atmospheric parameters and water-leaving reflectances are inverted through dedicated neural networks. TSM is produced via the latter. One output of the ocean color processing is a set of bio-geophysical products, including TSM, derived from the water-leaving reflectance (and associated error) using a neural net; these products are particularly focused on more complex Case 2 waters (typically along coasts) in which additional constituents must be considered (scattering by total suspended matter as well as absorption by detrital and Gelbstoff material). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-3-olci/level-2/ocean-processing), as well as the [Product User Guide](https://www.globcolour.info/CDR_Docs/GlobCOLOUR_PUG.pdf). ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. In addition to monthly TSM, GlobColour also offers daily and 8-day versions. GlobColour generates similar Level-3 (merged Level-2) products for a large number of biological parameters, such as particulate inorganic carbon and primary production, as well as atmospheric and ocean optical parameters. Collectively these are too numerous to list here. The full set can be found in the [Product User's Guide](https://www.globcolour.info/CDR_Docs/GlobCOLOUR_PUG.pdf). ### Visualizing the Data Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/ocn_011_nrt_rw0_total_suspended_matter). ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

description: _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](11f16cb9-def0-4bd5-a60e-50c542b837e3) as a replacement.**_ The AIS Annual Fishing Activity data set, produced by Global Fishing Watch, shows the distribution of time spent fishing in different locations throughout the ocean at a 0.01 degree resolution between 2012 and 2016. The time spent fishing in each pixel is tracked using a maritime Automatic Identification System (AIS), which is a radio communications system through which vessels continuously broadcast their identity and position using radio signals. Around 300,000 fishing vessels are tracked using this AIS system. From the AIS data, machine-learning classifiers are used to determine the type of ship, its size, what kind of fishing gear it uses, and where and when it is fishing based on its movement patterns. Fishing vessel gear types include six categories: 1) drifting longlines; 2) purse seines (pelagic and demersal); 3) trawlers (all types); 4) fixed_gear (set longlines, set gillnets, and pots and traps); 5) squid jiggers (mostly large industrial pelagic operating vessels); 6) other fishing (a combination of vessels of unknown fishing gear and other, less common gears such as trollers or pole and line). This data set shows the sum of hours spent fishing of each rig type to give the total fishing hours of all rig types. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. ### Overview The Predicted Vulnerability of Fisheries to Climate Change dataset shows the predicted vulnerability of marine capture fishing industries in 147 coastal countries for the time period of 2016-2050. Fishery vulnerabilities are presented at a national resolution with each country receiving a vulnerability score between 0 and 1, with the latter being the highest vulnerability. The dataset utilizes the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) definition of vulnerability, which is based on three variables: exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity. Additionally, the dataset used future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the IPCC’s Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5 to include the effect of climate change. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in current greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Marine ecosystems and fisheries provide a crucial foundation for human well-being and development, yielding 81.5 million tons of catch in 2014, valued at over $90 billion. For many [low-income food-deficit countries](http://www.fao.org/countryprofiles/lifdc/en/#:~:text=Three%20countries%20have%20graduated%20out,the%20net%20food%2Dexporter%20criterion) and local communities in developing countries, near-shore marine fisheries also provide a crucial source of micronutrients, which are necessary for early childhood development and influence long-term public health outcomes. The goal of this dataset is to provide a useful tool for understanding which countries are most at risk to the negative effects of climate change on the fishing industry in the coming decades. It can help prioritize the allocation of [climate finance](https://unfccc.int/topics/climate-finance/resources/biennial-assessment-of-climate-finance), as well as activities aimed at capacity building and the transfer of marine technology. The dataset was created by [Blasiak et al.](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/file?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0179632&type=printable), with additional help and grants from Stockholm University, University of Tokyo, James Cook University, and University of Waterloo. ### Methodology The Fisheries Vulnerability to Climate Change dataset was created by using the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) definition of vulnerability. Vulnerability was calculated by finding the difference between adaptive capacity and the sum of exposure and sensitivity. The **exposure** of countries to the impacts of climate change on marine capture fisheries was calculated based on projected sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies. SST anomalies were calculated by subtracting future SST average estimates by historical SST averages. Future SST estimates were taken from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) climate model for RCP 8.5 and averaged for the time period between 2016 to 2050. Historical reference climatology was also taken from the CMIP5 model from the year 1900 to 1950. SST anomaly data was then averaged among country boundaries to provide SST anomaly data by country. The index was then normalized on a scale of zero to one. The **sensitivity** or dependence of countries on marine capture fisheries was calculated as an index of five variables: number of fishers, share of marine fisheries exports in total exports, percentage of fishers in the economically active population, weight of total fisheries landings, and share of marine fish protein in total protein consumption. Data for the five variables was collected from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Bank Group and the World Factbook by the Central Intelligence Agency. Values for each variable were normalized on a scale from zero to one, and the five variables were averaged with equal weights. The total average value was then normalized on a scale from zero to one to create the sensitivity index. The **adaptive capacity** of countries represents the ability to modify or adjust fisheries and livelihoods in order to cope with the negative impacts of climate change and pursue any emerging opportunities. Six variables were combined to calculate the index of adaptive capacity: - Fisheries subsidies, collected from the Sea Around Us - Ratio of industrial to small-scale fisheries, collected from the Sea Around Us - Healthy life expectancy, taken from the World Health Organization (WHO) - Governance capacity (averaging six dimensions of governance), taken from the World Bank Group’s Worldwide Governance Indicators - Education levels (literacy rates or school enrollment rates), taken from the World Bank Group - Gross domestic product (GDP) per capita, taken from the World Bank Group’s Development Indicators database The mean of the two fisheries-related variables, fisheries subsidies and ratio of industrial to small-scale fisheries, made up one half of the adaptive capacity index. The four remaining socio-economic variables made up the other half of the adaptive capacity index. This gave the fisheries-related variables a greater weight than the socio-economic variables. The adaptive capacity index was then normalized on a scale from zero to one. The vulnerability index was calculated by finding the difference between the adaptive capacity and the sum of exposure and sensitivity, in line with the IPCC framework. The resulting vulnerability index was normalized on a scale from zero to one. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Indices for this same time period are available from the data provider for RCPs 2.6 and 4.5. Additionally, for the time period of 2066-2100, indices were calculated under the same three emissions scenarios (RCPs 2.6, 4.5, and 8.5). The FAO AQUASTAT Water Institutions database describes the various institutions in place in each country to manage water-related issues. The names of these institutions are listed, along with their type (government, university, etc.), sector (agriculture, irrigation, water, environment, natural resources, etc.) and activities (policy and strategy, infrastructure development, research, etc.). This information is updated at least every 5 years as FAO AQUASTAT performs country updates.

### Overview This is the first global inventory of commercial, industrial and utility scale solar energy stations. It has located nearly 70,000 facilities around the world, and has enriched this data with facility installation dates, previous land use, and proximity to conservation and indigenous protected areas. This dataset covers solar energy stations between June 2016 to October 2018. The solar installation location data is critical for improving the accuracy of current inventories and future forecasting, helping countries to align their energy systems to their net zero targets. When combined with weather data, the generating behaviour of precisely-located solar generating facilities becomes more predictable, allowing a larger share of total power generation to come from solar energy.The data will also help to ascertain the impact of solar installations on the natural and human-made world. The planet-scale study carried out by the team reveals some differences between top-down estimates of solar photovoltaic energy generating capacity reported by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the new bottom-up asset-level inventory. More generating capacity has been found in the United States (7,639 facilities, 54.1 GW), for example, than reported in top-down inventories (40.2GW), however the inventory for China (18,449 facilities,167.4 GW) almost precisely matches top-down estimates (173.5 GW). This dataset was developed by the University of Oxford, Descartes Lab, and the World Resources Institute (WRI). ### Additional Information Resource Watch also shows [global power plants](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Powerwatch) from this research team. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. ### Disclaimer Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata.

The Protected Connected (ProtConn) indicator shows the percentage of a country or region covered by protected connected lands. This data set, developed by the Digital Observatory for Protected Areas (DOPA) of the European Commission Joint Research Centre (EC JRC), provides the ProtConn value for each country and terrestrial ecoregion of the world, quantifying how well the terrestrial protected area systems in each country or ecoregion are designed to support connectivity. This data set provides the first global assessment of progress towards the protected area connectivity element of Aichi Target 11 of the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity that is to have at least 17% of the land covered by well-connected protected area systems by 2020. ProtConn was calculated using the public version of the World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) of June 2016 (only protected areas with a size of at least 1 km²) and, for the ecoregion layer, the ecoregion maps produced by Olsen, D.M. et al. 2001. While the range of median dispersal distances, or the typical distance between an individuals’ birth site to breeding site, ranges from 1 to 100 km for most terrestrial vertebrate species, the ProtConn values here shown are those corresponding to a species median dispersal distance of 10 km. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information (including results for other median dispersal distances like 1 km or 100 km), see the Learn More link. ### Additional Information Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The data set was created and published by Rob McDonald and The Nature Conservancy from research on water utilities and their annual reports. For each intake location, spatial location was recorded. ### Overview The Urban Land Use (Areal) – India dataset provides an estimation of land use land cover (LULC) for urban spaces in India. Maps are available for the years 2016 and 2019. Land cover indicates the physical cover over the surface of lands, such as water or vegetation, whereas land use shows how people use the land, such as commercial or plantation. A LULC map classifies areas within a set of categories. This dataset includes the following six categories: Open space, Nonresidential, Residential - Atomistic, Residential - Informal subdivision, Residential - Formal subdivision, and Residential - Housing project. These "areal" categories exclude the major "linear" urban LULC category: Roads. The final product has a resolution of 5 meters (m). The dataset was produced by the World Resources Institute (WRI). It provides an insight into LULC within cities: what lies where and when. This information can play a critical role in urban planning and monitoring. Example uses might be measuring the impact of different types of urban land use on air quality or identifying what types of land use have been affected by disasters. There is also a high value to change detection over time, looking both forward, for planning purposes, and backward, to chart and understand the outcomes of past pressures, development, and policy decisions. ### Methodology The Urban Land Use (Areal) – India dataset provides an estimation of land use land cover (LULC) for urban spaces in India. _**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](faaf0a0f-7475-49f3-bb8b-68edfaad4b77) as a replacement.**_ The Environmental Performance Index (EPI), produced by the Yale Center for Environmental Law and Policy (YCELP), Data-Driven Yale, and the Columbia University Earth Institute Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CEISIN), scores countries from 0 to 100 according to each country's relative performance on a set of environmental indicators. A score of 100 means that the country ranks above a high-quality benchmark for all its indicators. A score of 0 means that the country ranks below some low-quality benchmark for all its indicators. The index is built from 19 national-level indicators relevant to environmental issues, grouped into 9 issues, which are themselves divided into 2 overarching themes: (1) ecosystem vitality and (2) environmental health as it applies to human health. Multiple other data sets were employed to provide context before whittling down to those 19. Each country's score for each indicator is scaled between 0 and 100 to reflect the proximity of its score in that indicator to a high-quality benchmark. The high-quality benchmark can either be a statistical measure—such as the 95th percentile of the distribution of all countries' scores—or a scientifically determined target, such as the World Health Organization's designation of safe and dangerous amounts of particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5) in the air we breathe. The 19 indicators, each scored been 0 and 100, are then combined with each other to produce the overall EPI score for a country. The indicators are weighted differently depending on the relative reliability of the data that underpin them. A "materiality threshold" is used to determine whether an indicator should count toward a given country's score. Landlocked countries, for example, are not rated according to their marine protected areas or the health of their fisheries. When these indicators are removed, the remaining indicators receive proportionally higher weights in calculating the country total EPI. The EPI uses both primary and secondary data. Primary data come from human-administered surveys or technological monitoring schemes, including data derived from satellites. Secondary data include country-collected statistics, but only when those statistics are submitted to an independent international organization that enforces data reporting and quality requirements. Modeled data are also included. The 2016 global data set is retrieved from the Global Metrics for the Environment—2016 Environmental Performance Index Report. The FAO AQUASTAT Water Institutions database describes approximately 1,000 main institutions within 117 countries dealing with water resources for agriculture and rural development. Information is gathered in each country during the country update processes. The existing list of institutions is then provided with the request to add institutions that have come into existence since the last update, to delete institutions that don't exist anymore (and, if applicable, to replace them with their successors), and/or to add missing information for existing institutions. All institutions are recorded in the institution database. The names of these institutions are listed, along with their type (government, university, etc.), sector (agriculture, irrigation, water, environment, natural resources, etc.), and activities (policy and strategy, infrastructure development, research, etc.). Updates are continuous, whenever new data become available, but mainly during the country update, which takes place once every 5 years at the most. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. The Seasonal Trajectories product is a 10m, filtered time series of Plant Phenology Index (PPI), with regular time step, part of the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (CLMS) HR-VPP product suite. Plant Phenology Index (PPI) is a physically based vegetation index that is optimized for monitoring vegetation phenology and has a linear relationship with green leaf area index. The Seasonal Trajectories (ST) products are derived from a function fitting of the time series of the PPI vegetation index and hence provide a filtered PPI time series, with regular 10-day time step, together with related quality information (QFLAG). The PPI Seasonal Trajectories are derived from the PPI vegetation index and hence based on Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite observations. The ST products are made available as a set of raster files with 10 x 10m resolution, in UTM/WGS84 projection corresponding to the Sentinel-2 tiling grid, for those tiles that cover the EEA38 countries and the United Kingdom, and for the period from 2017 until today, with yearly updates. These Seasonal Trajectories are part of the pan-European High Resolution Vegetation Phenology and Productivity (HR-VPP) component of the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (CLMS).

description: Vegetation Phenology and Productivity (VPP) comprise 13 parameters up to 2 seasons that characterize the vegetation growth cycle. It is part of the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (CLMS) HR-VPP product suite. A set of 13 Vegetation Phenology and Productivity parameters are derived, for up to two growing seasons. These parameters include the start, end and length of the growing season, the dates when the vegetation index reaches its minimum and maximum values, the maximum value itself and its distance to the minimum (amplitude), the slopes of the green-up and green-down periods and the seasonal and total productivity. The Vegetation and Productivity parameters are extracted from the filtered PPI time-series, the HR-VPP Seasonal Trajectories, and hence based on Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite observations. The VPP parameters are made available as a set of raster files with 10 x 10m resolution, in UTM/WGS84 projection corresponding to the Sentinel-2 tiling grid, for those tiles that cover the EEA38 countries and the United Kingdom and for the period from 2017 until today, with yearly updates. This VPP product is part of the pan-European High Resolution Vegetation Phenology and Productivity (HR-VPP) component of the Copernicus Land Monitoring Service (CLMS).

description: Note: This Generation 1 Collection has been superseded by Generation 2 Simulation-level Collections The DestinE Digital Twin for Climate Change Adaptation (Climate DT) supports adaptation activities by providing innovative climate information on multi-decadal timescales, globally, at scales at which many impacts of climate change are observed. It combines cutting-edge global Earth-system models, impact-sector applications and observations into a unified framework to provide global climate projections and impact-sector information on multi-decadal timescales (1990 to ~2050), at very high spatial resolutions (5 to 10 km). The Climate DT represents the first ever attempt to operationalise the production of global multi-decadal climate projections, leveraging the world-leading supercomputing facilities of the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking along with some of the leading European climate models. A concise overview of what the Climate DT aims to achieve, and of the different concepts essential for an understanding of the Digital Twin’s characteristics, is included in the [Climate DT factsheet](https://destine.ecmwf.int/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/2024.06.07_Climate-DT-Fact-Sheet_V7-2.pdf) ## Storyline Simulation Present Climate Storyline simulations offer a what-if capability to explore how a weather event we experienced in the recent past would change in a warmer climate and how it would have looked in past pre-industrial conditions. To constrain simulated weather events, a nudging approach is used to keep the simulated large-scale flow close to the ERA5 reanalysis for the period 2017 – 2023. Processes on smaller scales and thermodynamic processes are free to evolve, which allows scientists to study e.g. how extreme precipitation would change in a warmer world for a weather event observed in present-day conditions. Initial conditions are taken from ocean-only spinup simulations for 1950 and 2017, and from the IFS-FESOM projection for a +2 °C world. Storyline simulations will be updated regularly to include most recent months. The next update will extend all storylines to include 2024. ## Models The Climate DT exploits and further evolves a new generation of global storm-resolving and eddy-rich models built through a cooperative model development approach. For more information on models please click [here](https://destine.ecmwf.int/climate-change-adaptation-digital-twin-climate-dt/#models) ## Simulations The Climate DT team carries out several types of digital twin simulations on the EuroHPC supercomputers. Multi-decadal simulations are produced to cover the recent past (from 1990) and possible future evolutions of the climate up to 2050. See [here](https://destine.ecmwf.int/climate-change-adaptation-digital-twin-climate-dt/#simulations) for more information on Simulations ## Parameters Below we see the list of parameters extracted from the 'DestinE Climate DT data portfolio', for more information please refer to the page [Climate DT Phase 1 CLTE Parameters](https://confluence.ecmwf.int/display/DDCZ/Climate+DT+Phase+1+data+catalogue)

description: The DestinE Digital Twin for Climate Change Adaptation (Climate DT) supports adaptation activities by providing innovative climate information on multi-decadal timescales, globally, at scales at which many impacts of climate change are observed. It combines cutting-edge global Earth-system models, impact-sector applications and observations into a unified framework to provide global climate projections and impact-sector information on multi-decadal timescales (1990 to ~2050), at very high spatial resolutions (5 to 10 km). The Climate DT represents the first ever attempt to operationalise the production of global multi-decadal climate projections, leveraging the world-leading supercomputing facilities of the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking along with some of the leading European climate models. A concise overview of what the Climate DT aims to achieve, and of the different concepts essential for an understanding of the Digital Twin’s characteristics, is included in the [Climate DT factsheet](https://destine.ecmwf.int/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/2024.06.07_Climate-DT-Fact-Sheet_V7-2.pdf) ## Storyline Simulation Present Climate Storyline simulations offer a what-if capability to explore how a weather event we experienced in the recent past would change in a warmer climate and how it would have looked in past pre-industrial conditions. To constrain simulated weather events, a nudging approach is used to keep the simulated large-scale flow close to the ERA5 reanalysis for the period 2017 – 2023. Processes on smaller scales and thermodynamic processes are free to evolve, which allows scientists to study e.g. how extreme precipitation would change in a warmer world for a weather event observed in present-day conditions. Initial conditions are taken from ocean-only spinup simulations for 1950 and 2017, and from the IFS-FESOM projection for a +2 °C world. Storyline simulations will be updated regularly to include most recent months. The next update will extend all storylines to include 2024. ## Models The Climate DT exploits and further evolves a new generation of global storm-resolving and eddy-rich models built through a cooperative model development approach.
